days.title: AWS SDK Fundamentals and API Design Basics

concepts.heading: SDK-Managed Retries and Exponential Backoff
concepts.body: Every official AWS SDK ships with a retry layer that automatically resends a failed request when the failure looks transient, such as a network blip or a service returning HTTP 500/503. Instead of retrying at a fixed interval, the SDK waits progressively longer between attempts (exponential backoff) and adds random jitter so that many clients recovering from the same outage do not all retry at exactly the same moment. Developers can tune this behavior through settings like maxAttempts and retryMode (legacy, standard, or adaptive) rather than writing custom retry loops. On the exam, a question describing sporadic failures that self-resolve almost always points to relying on or tuning this built-in mechanism rather than disabling retries.

concepts.heading: Designing Idempotent Operations
concepts.body: An idempotent operation produces the same end result no matter how many times the identical request is executed, which matters because network timeouts make it impossible for a client to know if a request that appears to have failed actually succeeded on the server. The standard pattern is to generate a unique idempotency key (often a UUID) on the client and pass it with the request; the server checks whether it has already processed that key before creating a new resource or charge. This is essential for payment and order-creation APIs, where a retried request must not create a duplicate charge or duplicate order. Without idempotency keys, naive retry logic combined with at-least-once delivery guarantees can silently corrupt business data.

concepts.heading: The Credential Provider Chain
concepts.body: AWS SDKs resolve credentials by walking a fixed provider chain in order: explicit code-level credentials, environment variables, the shared credentials/config file, and finally an IAM role attached to the compute environment (EC2 instance profile, ECS task role, or Lambda execution role). This ordering lets the same code run unmodified in a developer's laptop (using a local profile) and in production (using an attached IAM role), which is why hardcoding access keys in source code is considered an anti-pattern and a security risk. On EC2, credentials are actually fetched from the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) and rotated automatically. Exam questions that describe credentials being hardcoded or leaked are almost always testing whether you know to replace them with an IAM role instead.

concepts.heading: Handling Client and Server Errors Correctly
concepts.body: HTTP-based AWS APIs distinguish between 4xx errors, which mean the request itself was invalid (bad parameters, missing permissions, malformed JSON) and will fail identically no matter how many times you retry it, and 5xx errors or HTTP 429, which indicate a transient server-side or throttling problem that may well succeed on a later attempt. The AWS SDK's built-in retry logic already understands this distinction and will not waste attempts retrying a 4xx, while it will automatically back off and retry a 429 or 500-class error. A well-written application should still surface 4xx errors immediately to the caller with an actionable message rather than looping on them. Recognizing which status code family a described symptom falls into is often the fastest way to eliminate wrong answer choices on scenario questions.

concepts.heading: RESTful API Design Principles
concepts.body: A well-designed REST API models data as resources addressed by nouns in the URL path (for example /orders/123/items) and uses HTTP verbs to express the action: GET to read, POST to create, PUT/PATCH to update, and DELETE to remove, while remaining stateless so that no session context is stored on the server between requests. Consistent use of standard HTTP status codes (200, 201, 400, 403, 404, 429, 500) lets client SDKs and API Gateway apply generic error handling without inspecting response bodies. This design discipline becomes directly relevant once you place Amazon API Gateway in front of Lambda or another backend, because Gateway's request/response mapping, validation, and throttling features all assume a resource-oriented, verb-driven API shape.

examPoints: A question describing an application that occasionally fails calls with HTTP 429 or 500 responses that succeed moments later is testing whether you know the SDK's exponential backoff and jitter already handle this, rather than requiring you to disable or bypass retries.

A scenario about a payment or order API where a network timeout causes the client to resend an identical request, and duplicate charges or duplicate orders must be avoided, is a direct pointer to implementing an idempotency key.

quiz.q: A checkout service occasionally times out waiting for a payment API response, and the client automatically resubmits the exact same request. How should the team prevent the resubmission from creating a duplicate charge?
choices: Increase the client-side timeout so retries happen less often
Generate an idempotency key on the client and have the payment service deduplicate requests by that key
Disable all client-side retries
Reduce the payment API's throttling limit
quiz.explain: An idempotency key lets the server recognize that a retried request is a duplicate of one it already processed and return the original result instead of creating a new charge; simply disabling retries (choice C) would just turn transient failures into visible errors for the user without solving the duplication risk.

quiz.q: An application using the AWS SDK begins receiving HTTP 429 responses from a downstream AWS service during a traffic spike. What does the SDK do by default?
choices: It immediately throws an exception with no retry
It retries the request automatically using exponential backoff with jitter
It retries every 1 millisecond until it succeeds
It silently drops the request and returns a cached response
quiz.explain: AWS SDKs include built-in retry logic with exponential backoff and jitter specifically to handle throttling (429) and transient server errors; option C describes a tight retry loop, which is the opposite of what backoff is designed to prevent.

days.recap: The SDK bakes in retry/backoff for transient errors, idempotency keys stop duplicate side effects from retries, credentials resolve via a fixed provider chain ending in IAM roles, and 4xx vs 5xx/429 determines whether retrying makes sense at all.

days.title: API Gateway Integration Types, Caching, and Throttling

concepts.heading: Lambda Proxy Integration vs Other Integration Types
concepts.body: API Gateway supports several integration types: Lambda proxy integration forwards the entire raw HTTP request to Lambda and expects a specifically shaped response object back, giving the function full control over headers, status codes, and body; Lambda custom (non-proxy) integration instead lets API Gateway transform the request and response with mapping templates. HTTP integration proxies calls straight to another HTTP endpoint, AWS service integration calls an AWS API directly (such as writing to DynamoDB) with no Lambda in between, and mock integration returns a canned response for testing only. Lambda proxy integration is the most common choice because it keeps transformation logic in application code rather than gateway-side templates, which is easier to test and version.

concepts.heading: Reducing Backend Load with API Gateway Caching
concepts.body: API Gateway can cache responses for a configurable time-to-live per stage, so repeated identical requests are served from the cache instead of invoking the backend again, cutting both latency and cost. The cache key combines the request path with whichever query string parameters or headers you explicitly mark as part of it, so two requests differing only in an ignored parameter hit the same cache entry. Caching is billed hourly based on provisioned cache size and suits read-heavy, slowly-changing data; clients with the right permissions can also invalidate it early. A common exam trap is caching an endpoint whose data changes on every request, which would return stale results instead of helping.

concepts.heading: Throttling to Protect the Backend
concepts.body: API Gateway enforces throttling at the account level, and you can override those limits at the stage or even individual method level, expressed as a steady-state requests-per-second rate and a burst capacity using a token bucket algorithm. This protects downstream systems like Lambda or a database from being overwhelmed by a traffic spike, returning HTTP 429 to callers once the limit is exceeded. On top of account/stage throttling, Usage Plans paired with API keys let you throttle and quota individual clients or partners independently of one another, which is the mechanism to use when only one noisy client should be restricted without affecting everyone else. Usage plans also support per-method quotas (e.g., 10,000 requests per day) in addition to rate limits.

concepts.heading: REST APIs vs HTTP APIs
concepts.body: API Gateway offers two API types: REST APIs, which support the full feature set including request validation, API keys, usage plans, caching, and AWS WAF integration, and HTTP APIs, a newer, lighter-weight option that is cheaper and has lower latency but lacks some of those advanced features (notably, HTTP APIs historically lack built-in caching and have more limited request transformation). HTTP APIs do support JWT authorizers natively and are a strong default choice for simple proxy-to-Lambda use cases where cost and latency matter more than deep customization. Choosing between the two on the exam usually comes down to spotting a feature the scenario needs (caching, usage plans, WAF) that only REST APIs provide.

concepts.heading: Request Validation and Custom Domain Names
concepts.body: API Gateway can validate incoming requests against a JSON Schema model before ever invoking the backend, rejecting malformed payloads with a 400 error and saving Lambda invocations (and cost) on requests that would fail anyway. Custom domain names let you expose an API under your own domain instead of the default execute-api URL, requiring an ACM certificate that must be requested in us-east-1 for edge-optimized custom domains or in the API's own region for regional custom domains. Combining request validation with throttling and caching gives you a defense-in-depth strategy for a public-facing API: bad requests are rejected early, abusive clients are throttled, and repeated valid requests are served from cache.

examPoints: A scenario describing the same read-heavy, rarely-changing query hitting the backend repeatedly and driving up latency or cost points to enabling API Gateway response caching, not to scaling the backend itself.

A scenario where one specific partner or client is overwhelming the API while other clients must be unaffected points to a Usage Plan with a per-client API key, rather than adjusting the account- or stage-wide throttle.

quiz.q: A read-heavy endpoint returns the same product catalog data on most requests, and the team wants to reduce backend load and latency without changing the Lambda function. What should they configure?
choices: Lower the API Gateway account-level throttle
Enable API Gateway caching on the stage with an appropriate TTL
Switch the integration to mock integration
Increase the Lambda function's reserved concurrency
quiz.explain: Stage-level caching serves repeated identical requests directly from API Gateway without invoking the backend; lowering the throttle (choice A) would only make the API reject more requests, not reduce backend load for legitimate traffic.

quiz.q: One partner's integration is making far more requests than expected and API Gateway is starting to throttle other well-behaved clients as a result. What is the best fix?
choices: Disable throttling for the entire API
Create a Usage Plan with a dedicated API key and per-client quota for that partner
Ask all clients to reduce their request rate
Move the API to a different AWS region
quiz.explain: Usage Plans with API keys let you isolate rate limits and quotas per client, so the noisy partner can be constrained without a blanket throttle change affecting everyone else.

days.recap: API Gateway integration types range from Lambda proxy to direct AWS service calls, caching cuts backend load for repeat reads, account/stage throttling protects the backend while Usage Plans throttle individual clients, and REST APIs trade cost for the fuller feature set HTTP APIs lack.

days.title: Event-Driven Architecture with SQS, SNS, and EventBridge

concepts.heading: Amazon SQS: Point-to-Point Decoupling
concepts.body: Amazon SQS is a point-to-point message queue: a producer sends a message into the queue and exactly one consumer pulls and processes it, after which the message is deleted (standard queues) or, in FIFO queues, processed in strict order with exactly-once processing within a message group. This is the foundational building block for decoupling a fast producer from a slower or intermittently available consumer, since the queue absorbs bursts and lets the consumer work through the backlog at its own pace. A message that a consumer fails to delete within its visibility timeout becomes visible again for another consumer to pick up, which is how SQS handles worker crashes without losing messages. Because only one consumer ultimately processes each message, SQS is not the right tool when multiple independent systems each need their own copy of an event.

concepts.heading: Amazon SNS: Publish/Subscribe Fan-Out
concepts.body: Amazon SNS implements the publish/subscribe pattern: a publisher sends a single message to an SNS topic, and SNS delivers a copy of that message to every subscriber, which can be SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP/HTTPS endpoints, email, or SMS. This makes SNS the natural choice whenever one event needs to reach multiple independent consumers simultaneously, as opposed to SQS where only one consumer would receive it. Message filtering policies on subscriptions let each subscriber receive only the subset of messages it cares about, based on message attributes, without the publisher needing to know about individual subscribers.

concepts.heading: The SNS + SQS Fan-Out Pattern
concepts.body: Combining SNS and SQS is one of the most tested architecture patterns on this exam: a single SNS topic fans out to multiple SQS queues, one per downstream system, so that each system processes the same event independently and at its own pace, and a failure or slowdown in one consumer's queue has zero effect on the others. This also adds durability that raw SNS-to-HTTP subscriptions lack, because if a consumer is temporarily unavailable, its messages simply wait safely in its SQS queue rather than being lost. This pattern is the standard answer whenever a scenario describes one business event (like 'order placed') that must independently trigger inventory, notification, and analytics processing.

concepts.heading: Amazon EventBridge: Rule-Based Event Routing
concepts.body: Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event bus that ingests events from AWS services, custom applications, and SaaS partners, then routes them to one or more targets based on rules that match against the event's JSON structure using event patterns (not simple topic names). A single custom event bus can support many independent rules, each filtering for different event shapes and routing to different targets like Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, or Kinesis, which makes EventBridge far more flexible for routing heterogeneous events than SNS's topic-based model. EventBridge also supports scheduled rules (cron or rate expressions) for time-based triggers and an integrated schema registry that can infer the structure of events flowing through a bus.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between SNS, SQS, and EventBridge
concepts.body: The decision usually comes down to shape and source of the traffic: use SQS alone for simple one-to-one work queues, use SNS (often with SQS fan-out) when you control the publisher and need to broadcast one type of event to many known subscribers, and use EventBridge when events originate from many different sources (including third-party SaaS applications) and need content-based routing rules rather than a fixed subscriber list. EventBridge and SNS can also be combined, for example when an EventBridge rule needs to notify a human via SMS or email, since EventBridge itself does not support those endpoint types directly.

examPoints: A scenario where a single event (such as an order being placed) must trigger independent processing in several unrelated downstream systems, each of which should be unaffected by the others' failures, is the classic SNS-to-multiple-SQS fan-out pattern.

A scenario involving events from multiple SaaS partners or various AWS services that need to be filtered by content and routed to different targets is pointing to Amazon EventBridge and its rule-based event pattern matching, not SNS topics.

quiz.q: An 'order placed' event must independently trigger inventory updates, a customer notification, and a downstream analytics pipeline, and a failure in one of these systems must not block or delay the others. Which design meets this requirement?
choices: A single SQS queue consumed in turn by all three systems
An SNS topic with a separate SQS queue subscribed for each of the three systems
Three synchronous REST calls made directly from the order service
A single Lambda function that calls all three systems in sequence
quiz.explain: The SNS fan-out pattern delivers an independent copy of the event to each subscribed SQS queue, so each consumer processes at its own pace and a failure in one queue's consumer has no effect on the others; a single shared SQS queue (choice A) would let only one consumer process each message, not all three.

quiz.q: A company ingests events from several SaaS vendors and multiple AWS accounts, and needs to filter and route them to different Lambda functions based on the event's content. Which service is purpose-built for this?
choices: Amazon SQS standard queue
Amazon EventBridge with content-based event pattern rules
Amazon SNS with a single topic
AWS Direct Connect
quiz.explain: EventBridge is designed to ingest events from many heterogeneous sources, including SaaS partners, and route them using flexible content-based pattern matching; SNS routes by topic subscription, not by inspecting event content.

days.recap: SQS delivers each message to exactly one consumer for decoupled work queues, SNS fans a message out to every subscriber, SNS+SQS combines both for independent multi-consumer processing, and EventBridge adds content-based routing across many event sources.

days.title: Lambda Fundamentals: Handlers, Layers, Versions, and Aliases

concepts.heading: The Lambda Execution Model and Handler
concepts.body: A Lambda function's handler is the entry point the Lambda runtime invokes for every event; it receives an event object containing the input payload and a context object exposing metadata such as the remaining execution time, the AWS request ID, and the function's ARN. Lambda automatically provisions and manages the underlying compute (an execution environment) to run this handler, scaling out by launching additional parallel execution environments as concurrent invocations increase, with each environment processing one invocation at a time (outside of response streaming scenarios). Code and any objects declared outside the handler function persist across invocations within the same warm execution environment, which is why developers initialize expensive resources like database clients at the module/global level rather than inside the handler.

concepts.heading: Lambda Layers for Shared Dependencies
concepts.body: A Lambda layer is a .zip archive containing libraries, a custom runtime, or other dependencies that can be attached to multiple functions, letting you avoid packaging the same third-party libraries into every function's deployment package. This both shrinks individual deployment packages (helpful for staying under Lambda's size limits) and centralizes dependency updates, since updating a layer version and pointing functions at the new version is simpler than redeploying every function. A function can reference up to five layers, and layer content is extracted into /opt in the execution environment, so code needs to import dependencies from paths under /opt rather than assuming they are bundled alongside the handler.

concepts.heading: Environment Variables and Configuration
concepts.body: Lambda environment variables let you inject configuration (feature flags, table names, endpoint URLs) into a function without changing code, and they can be encrypted with a KMS key for values that are sensitive but do not need automatic rotation. For values that truly need rotation or that represent credentials, referencing AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store from the function at runtime is preferred over storing them as plain environment variables, since environment variables are visible to anyone with read access to the function's configuration. Environment variables are also commonly used to select behavior per deployment stage, such as pointing a 'staging' alias's underlying version at a different downstream table name than 'production'.

concepts.heading: Versions: Immutable Snapshots of Code
concepts.body: Publishing a Lambda version creates an immutable, numbered snapshot of the function's code and configuration exactly as they exist at that moment; the special $LATEST version continues to reflect whatever you deploy next, but numbered versions (1, 2, 3, ...) never change once published. This immutability is what makes versions safe to reference from other services or to roll back to, since you know precisely what code a given version number will always run, unlike $LATEST which can change under you.

concepts.heading: Aliases and Weighted Traffic Shifting
concepts.body: An alias is a named, mutable pointer to a specific function version (or, uniquely, to $LATEST), and callers invoke the alias ARN instead of a version number so that which version actually runs can change without updating every caller. Aliases support weighted routing across two versions simultaneously, for example sending 90% of invocations to version 5 and 10% to version 6, which is the mechanism behind canary and linear deployment strategies for Lambda; AWS CodeDeploy automates shifting that weight over time and can roll back automatically if CloudWatch alarms fire during the shift.

examPoints: A scenario where multiple Lambda functions need to share the same third-party library, and the team wants to shrink each function's deployment package and centralize updates, is pointing to Lambda Layers.

A scenario describing gradually shifting a small percentage of production traffic to a new Lambda version, with the ability to roll back automatically on error spikes, is pointing to an alias with weighted routing (typically automated with CodeDeploy).

quiz.q: Five Lambda functions all depend on the same internal logging library, and each function's deployment package is close to the size limit. What is the best way to reduce package size and centralize future updates to that library?
choices: Copy the library's source files into each function's package
Package the library as a Lambda Layer and attach it to each function
Store the library code as an environment variable
Create a separate alias for the library in each function
quiz.explain: A Lambda Layer is shared across functions and extracted separately at /opt, keeping each function's own package small; environment variables (choice C) cannot hold executable library code.

quiz.q: A team wants to send only 10% of production Lambda traffic to a newly published version, watch for errors, and route the remaining 90% to the previous version until confidence is established. What Lambda feature enables this directly?
choices: Publishing a new $LATEST version
An alias configured with weighted traffic routing across two versions
Increasing reserved concurrency
Enabling a Lambda Layer
quiz.explain: Aliases support splitting invocation traffic by percentage between two specific versions, which is the building block for canary-style rollouts; publishing a new version alone (choice A) does not shift any traffic by itself.

days.recap: The handler receives event and context on every invocation, Layers share dependencies across functions, versions are immutable snapshots while aliases are mutable pointers, and weighted alias routing enables canary-style traffic shifting.

days.title: Lambda Concurrency, Cold Starts, and Event Source Mapping

concepts.heading: Concurrency Scaling and Reserved Concurrency
concepts.body: Lambda scales by launching a separate execution environment for each concurrent invocation, up to your account's regional concurrency limit, which means a burst of 500 simultaneous requests can trigger up to 500 parallel executions without any capacity planning on your part. Reserved concurrency sets both a ceiling and a guaranteed minimum for a specific function: it prevents that function from ever exceeding a set number of concurrent executions (protecting downstream resources like a database connection pool) while also reserving that capacity away from the shared account pool so noisy neighbor functions cannot starve it. Setting reserved concurrency to zero effectively turns a function off, which is sometimes used deliberately as an emergency kill switch.

concepts.heading: Provisioned Concurrency to Eliminate Cold Starts
concepts.body: A cold start is the latency incurred when Lambda must initialize a brand-new execution environment: downloading code, starting the runtime, and running any initialization code outside the handler, which can add hundreds of milliseconds to seconds depending on runtime, package size, and whether the function is attached to a VPC. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes a specified number of execution environments ahead of time and keeps them warm, so invocations against that capacity skip the cold-start path entirely, which matters for latency-sensitive, user-facing APIs. Provisioned concurrency is billed separately from standard invocation charges, so it is deliberately applied only to functions where consistent low latency justifies the extra cost, often combined with Application Auto Scaling to scale the provisioned amount with a schedule or target utilization.

concepts.heading: Event Source Mapping for Poll-Based Triggers
concepts.body: For services that don't push events directly to Lambda, such as SQS, DynamoDB Streams, and Kinesis Data Streams, Lambda uses an internal poller called an event source mapping that continuously polls the source, batches up records, and invokes your function with the batch. You can tune batch size (how many records per invocation) and, for streams, a parallelization factor that allows multiple concurrent invocations per shard to increase throughput. For SQS, the event source mapping also respects the queue's visibility timeout, so it will not deliver the same message to a second concurrent invocation while an earlier one is still processing it.

concepts.heading: Dead-Letter Queues and On-Failure Destinations
concepts.body: When a Lambda function invoked via an SQS event source mapping repeatedly fails to process a message, the message becomes visible again after each visibility timeout expires and is retried, but after the queue's configured maxReceiveCount is reached, it is moved to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) instead of being retried forever, isolating poison-pill messages for offline inspection without blocking the rest of the queue. For asynchronous Lambda invocations (like those from S3 or SNS) rather than event-source-mapped ones, Lambda instead supports on-failure destinations (an SQS queue, SNS topic, another Lambda function, or EventBridge bus) that automatically receive the failed event's details, which is a more modern replacement for a DLQ in that context.

concepts.heading: Right-Sizing Memory to Control Both Cost and Speed
concepts.body: Lambda allocates CPU power proportionally to the memory setting you choose, so increasing memory can actually make a CPU-bound function finish faster and sometimes cost the same or less overall, since billing is based on memory allocated multiplied by execution duration. AWS Lambda Power Tuning (an open-source tool) and CloudWatch metrics are commonly used to find the memory setting that minimizes cost for a given function's workload rather than assuming that the lowest memory setting is always cheapest.

examPoints: A scenario describing a latency-sensitive, user-facing API backed by Lambda that must avoid cold-start delays entirely is pointing to Provisioned Concurrency, not merely increasing reserved concurrency (which only sets limits, not pre-warmed capacity).

A scenario about a critical Lambda function being starved of capacity because other functions in the same account are consuming all available concurrency is pointing to setting Reserved Concurrency on the critical function to guarantee it capacity.

quiz.q: A real-time bidding API backed by Lambda must respond within tight latency SLAs and cannot tolerate cold-start delays during traffic spikes. What should the team configure?
choices: Reserved concurrency set to the account maximum
Provisioned concurrency sized to expected peak traffic
A larger deployment package to improve caching
A dead-letter queue on the function
quiz.explain: Provisioned concurrency pre-warms execution environments so invocations bypass the cold-start path; reserved concurrency (choice A) only sets a ceiling and a guarantee on concurrent executions, it does not pre-initialize anything.

quiz.q: A Lambda function triggered by an SQS event source mapping keeps failing on the same message, and the team wants to stop it from blocking the rest of the queue while preserving the message for analysis. What should they configure?
choices: Set the SQS visibility timeout to zero
Configure a dead-letter queue with a maxReceiveCount on the source queue
Disable the event source mapping entirely
Increase the Lambda function's timeout to one hour
quiz.explain: A DLQ with maxReceiveCount automatically isolates a message after repeated failed processing attempts, letting the rest of the queue continue to flow; disabling the mapping (choice C) would stop all processing, not just the poison message.

days.recap: Reserved concurrency caps and guarantees a function's capacity, provisioned concurrency pre-warms environments to remove cold starts, event source mappings poll SQS/DynamoDB Streams/Kinesis on Lambda's behalf, and DLQs isolate repeatedly failing messages.

days.title: DynamoDB for Developers: Keys, Indexes, DAX, and Transactions

concepts.heading: Partition Keys, Sort Keys, and Access Pattern Design
concepts.body: DynamoDB distributes data across partitions based on the hash of the partition key, and within a partition, items are ordered by the sort key if one is defined, so a well-chosen key schema is the single biggest factor in DynamoDB performance. Because DynamoDB has no general-purpose secondary query language like SQL joins, you must design your keys around the specific access patterns your application needs (for example, PK=CustomerId, SK=OrderDate to fetch a customer's orders in date order) before you write any data, unlike a relational database where you can add ad hoc queries later. Choosing a partition key with low cardinality (few distinct values, like a status field) creates a 'hot partition' that concentrates traffic on one physical partition and throttles throughput, which is one of the most common real-world DynamoDB design mistakes.

concepts.heading: Global Secondary Indexes (GSI)
concepts.body: A Global Secondary Index lets you query the same table using a completely different partition key (and optionally sort key) than the base table, which is how you support a second access pattern, such as looking up orders by customer ID when the base table's primary key is order ID. A GSI has its own provisioned throughput (or scales independently under on-demand mode) and is only eventually consistent, meaning a write to the base table may take a short time to appear in the index. GSIs can be added or removed after the table already exists, which makes them the flexible go-to tool when a new access pattern emerges after the table is already in production.

concepts.heading: Local Secondary Indexes (LSI)
concepts.body: A Local Secondary Index keeps the same partition key as the base table but defines an alternate sort key, letting you sort or filter items within a partition differently, and unlike a GSI, an LSI supports strongly consistent reads. The major constraint is that LSIs must be defined at table creation time and cannot be added or removed later, and all LSIs on a table share the base table's provisioned throughput rather than having independent capacity, plus each partition is limited to 10GB when LSIs are in use. Because of this inflexibility, GSIs are chosen far more often in practice and on the exam unless a question specifically calls out a need for strong consistency on an alternate sort order.

concepts.heading: DynamoDB Transactions for Multi-Item Atomicity
concepts.body: TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems provide ACID transaction semantics across up to 100 items (or 4MB) spanning one or more tables in a single AWS account and region, guaranteeing that either every operation in the transaction succeeds or none of them do. This is the correct tool whenever a business operation must touch multiple items atomically, such as decrementing inventory count and creating an order record together, where a partial failure would leave the data inconsistent. Transactions consume roughly twice the write capacity of the equivalent non-transactional writes, which is a deliberate cost/consistency trade-off worth remembering.

concepts.heading: DynamoDB Streams and DAX
concepts.body: DynamoDB Streams captures a time-ordered sequence of item-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) that Lambda or the Kinesis Client Library can consume to trigger downstream reactions, such as replicating changes to another table, sending notifications, or maintaining a materialized view. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a separate, fully managed in-memory cache that sits in front of DynamoDB and can reduce read latency from single-digit milliseconds to microseconds for read-heavy workloads, requiring only a small SDK change (the DAX client is API-compatible with the DynamoDB client) rather than any application redesign; note that DAX caches at the API-call level and is eventually consistent, so it is not suitable when an application requires strongly consistent reads on every request.

examPoints: A scenario where an existing DynamoDB table needs to support a brand-new query pattern (a different key than the original design) after it is already in production is pointing to adding a Global Secondary Index, since GSIs (unlike LSIs) can be created after table creation.

A scenario requiring multiple items, possibly across tables, to succeed or fail together as a single atomic unit (such as inventory decrement plus order creation) is pointing to DynamoDB transactions (TransactWriteItems), not a sequence of individual PutItem calls.

quiz.q: An orders table was originally designed to be queried only by order ID, but the application now also needs to efficiently list all orders for a given customer. The table is already in production with live data. What should the team do?
choices: Recreate the table from scratch with a new key schema
Add a Global Secondary Index with customer ID as the partition key
Add a Local Secondary Index with customer ID as the partition key
Perform a full table Scan filtered by customer ID for every request
quiz.explain: GSIs can be added to a live table without disruption and support a completely different partition key, exactly matching this new access pattern; LSIs (choice C) cannot be added after table creation, ruling that option out.

quiz.q: An order-processing workflow must decrement product inventory and create a new order record such that both operations succeed together or neither takes effect. Which DynamoDB capability should be used?
choices: DynamoDB Streams
TransactWriteItems
A Global Secondary Index
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
quiz.explain: TransactWriteItems provides atomic, all-or-nothing writes across multiple items, which is exactly the guarantee this workflow needs; DynamoDB Streams (choice A) only reports on changes after they happen and provides no atomicity guarantee.

days.recap: Key design drives DynamoDB performance, GSIs add new query patterns after the fact with eventual consistency while LSIs require upfront planning for strong consistency, transactions guarantee atomicity across items, and DAX caches reads with microsecond latency.

days.title: Other Data Stores: RDS/Aurora, S3, and In-Memory Caching

concepts.heading: The Aurora Data API for Serverless SQL Access
concepts.body: The Aurora Data API provides an HTTP-based endpoint for running SQL statements against an Aurora Serverless database without opening or managing a traditional database connection, which is particularly valuable for Lambda functions that would otherwise need to manage a connection pool across many short-lived, highly concurrent executions. Because each call is a stateless HTTPS request authenticated with IAM, the Data API also removes the need to store or rotate database credentials for that access path, since authorization is governed by IAM policy instead. This is distinct from RDS Proxy, which pools traditional database connections rather than replacing them with an HTTP API; the two solve a similar underlying problem (Lambda's connection-scaling issues) in different ways.

concepts.heading: S3 Multipart Upload for Large Objects
concepts.body: Multipart upload splits a large object into independent parts that can be uploaded in parallel, retried individually if one part fails, and paused and resumed later, which is strongly recommended for any object larger than 100MB and required for objects over 5GB. This dramatically improves upload reliability and throughput over unstable or bandwidth-limited connections compared to uploading a single large object in one request, since a failure only requires re-sending the affected part rather than restarting from zero.

concepts.heading: Presigned URLs for Direct Client Access
concepts.body: A presigned URL is a URL generated by an application (using its own AWS credentials and the S3 SDK) that grants time-limited permission to perform a specific action, such as GET or PUT, directly against an S3 object, without the requester needing any AWS credentials of their own. This is the standard pattern for letting mobile or web clients upload user files (like profile photos) directly to S3, bypassing the application server entirely for the data transfer while the server still controls who is authorized to generate a URL and for how long it remains valid (specified in seconds at generation time).

concepts.heading: S3 Event Notifications for Automated Pipelines
concepts.body: S3 can publish an event notification the moment an object is created, deleted, or restored, delivering that event to Lambda, SQS, SNS, or EventBridge, which is the foundation of most 'upload triggers processing' pipelines, such as automatically generating a thumbnail after an image upload or kicking off a batch job after a data file lands in a bucket. EventBridge is now the recommended target for new designs because it supports richer filtering and multiple simultaneous rule-based destinations from the same bucket, whereas the original S3-to-Lambda/SQS/SNS notification configuration only supports a limited number of destinations per event type.

concepts.heading: ElastiCache vs MemoryDB
concepts.body: Amazon ElastiCache (supporting Redis OSS or Memcached engines) is primarily used as a fast, in-memory cache layered in front of a slower primary data store, and while Redis-mode ElastiCache does support some persistence and replication options, it is generally treated as a cache where data loss is tolerable because the source of truth lives elsewhere. Amazon MemoryDB for Redis, in contrast, is a Redis-compatible, durable, multi-AZ in-memory database designed to be used as a primary data store in its own right, using a distributed transactional log so that data survives node failures without needing a separate backing database. Choosing between them comes down to whether the in-memory data needs to be durable enough to be the system of record (MemoryDB) or is disposable and rebuildable from another source (ElastiCache).

examPoints: A scenario where a mobile client must upload a large file directly to S3 without holding any AWS credentials of its own is pointing to a presigned URL, not to relaxing the bucket's access controls or routing the upload through the application server.

A scenario describing a Lambda function that needs to run SQL queries against Aurora Serverless without managing database connection pooling is pointing to the Aurora Data API rather than a traditional JDBC/ODBC connection.

quiz.q: A mobile app needs users to upload photos directly to an S3 bucket without embedding any AWS credentials in the app and without routing the file bytes through the application's own servers. What should be used?
choices: Make the S3 bucket publicly writable
Generate a time-limited presigned URL for each upload
Hardcode a long-lived IAM access key into the mobile app
Have every client assume the same broad IAM role
quiz.explain: A presigned URL grants temporary, scoped permission to upload without exposing any credentials to the client; making the bucket publicly writable (choice A) would allow uploads from anyone, not just authenticated app users.

quiz.q: A team wants their Lambda functions to run SQL statements against an Aurora Serverless cluster without managing a JDBC connection pool across many concurrent short-lived invocations. What should they use?
choices: A direct JDBC connection opened fresh in every invocation
The Aurora Data API
Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
Amazon MemoryDB for Redis
quiz.explain: The Aurora Data API exposes SQL execution over a stateless HTTPS endpoint, removing the connection-pooling burden entirely; DAX (choice C) is a DynamoDB-specific cache and has nothing to do with Aurora.

days.recap: The Aurora Data API gives Lambda connection-free SQL access, S3 supports multipart uploads and presigned URLs for large/direct transfers, S3 event notifications drive upload-triggered pipelines, and MemoryDB (unlike ElastiCache) is durable enough to be a primary data store.

days.title: AppSync/GraphQL and Kinesis Data Streams Development

concepts.heading: AWS AppSync and the GraphQL Model
concepts.body: AWS AppSync is a fully managed GraphQL service that lets you define a single schema describing your data types and the queries, mutations, and subscriptions clients can perform, then attach resolvers that map each schema field to a data source such as DynamoDB, Lambda, RDS, or an HTTP endpoint. Because a GraphQL client specifies exactly which fields it wants in a single request, AppSync eliminates both over-fetching (receiving unused fields) and under-fetching (needing multiple round trips to assemble a screen's worth of data), which are common pain points with REST APIs backing complex mobile or web UIs.

concepts.heading: Real-Time Data with AppSync Subscriptions
concepts.body: AppSync subscriptions let a client register interest in a specific mutation and receive a push notification in real time over a managed WebSocket connection whenever that mutation occurs elsewhere, without the client needing to poll. This is the standard AWS-managed building block for real-time features like chat applications, live dashboards, or collaborative editing indicators, and it removes the need to build and scale your own WebSocket infrastructure.

concepts.heading: Offline Support and Conflict Resolution
concepts.body: AppSync includes built-in support for offline data access and synchronization through client SDKs (such as Amplify DataStore), which cache data locally and sync changes when connectivity returns, along with configurable conflict detection and resolution strategies (such as optimistic concurrency using a version field, or a custom Lambda resolver) for when the same record is modified while offline by more than one client.

concepts.heading: Kinesis Data Streams: Shards and the Client Library
concepts.body: Kinesis Data Streams ingests high-throughput, ordered records into shards, where each shard supports a fixed write and read throughput, and you scale total stream throughput by adding or splitting shards. Consumer applications typically use the Kinesis Client Library (KCL), which handles shard discovery, load balancing consumers across shards, and periodically checkpointing progress (usually to a DynamoDB table) so that a consumer restarting after a crash resumes from the last checkpoint rather than reprocessing the entire stream or losing records.

concepts.heading: Kinesis vs SQS for Streaming Workloads
concepts.body: The key architectural difference is that Kinesis retains records for a configurable period (24 hours by default, up to 365 days) and allows multiple independent consumer applications to each read the entire stream at their own pace and position, which is essential for use cases like simultaneous real-time analytics and long-term archival from the same data. SQS, in contrast, removes a message once it's successfully processed by a single consumer, which fits simple work-queue distribution but cannot support multiple independent 'replays' of the same event stream the way Kinesis can.

examPoints: A scenario describing a mobile or web client that needs to fetch data from several different backend sources in one request while retrieving only the specific fields it needs is pointing to AWS AppSync and GraphQL rather than composing multiple REST calls.

A scenario where the same real-time stream of events must be independently consumed and replayed by more than one application (for example, one doing real-time analytics and another archiving to S3) is pointing to Kinesis Data Streams, since SQS removes a message after one consumer processes it.

quiz.q: A mobile application needs real-time updates pushed to connected clients whenever a chat message is created, without building custom WebSocket server infrastructure. Which AWS service feature directly supports this?
choices: Amazon SQS long polling
AWS AppSync subscriptions
Amazon S3 event notifications
AWS Direct Connect
quiz.explain: AppSync subscriptions push mutation results to clients in real time over managed WebSocket connections; SQS long polling (choice A) requires clients to actively poll and is not a real-time push mechanism.

quiz.q: A clickstream data pipeline needs both a real-time fraud-detection application and a separate batch archival job to independently read every event from the same stream, each at its own pace. Which service fits this requirement?
choices: Amazon SQS standard queue
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
AWS AppSync
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration
quiz.explain: Kinesis retains records and allows multiple independent consumers to read the full stream at their own position, unlike SQS where a message disappears once one consumer processes it.

days.recap: AppSync unifies multiple data sources under one GraphQL schema and supports real-time subscriptions and offline sync, while Kinesis Data Streams uses shards and the KCL to let multiple independent consumers replay the same ordered stream.

days.title: Domain 1 Review: Development with AWS Services

concepts.heading: Messaging and Eventing Recap
concepts.body: Domain 1 opens with three messaging primitives that are frequently confused: SQS delivers each message to exactly one consumer for point-to-point decoupling, SNS fans a single message out to every subscriber for pub/sub broadcast, and EventBridge adds schema-aware, content-based routing across many heterogeneous event sources including SaaS partners. The SNS-plus-SQS fan-out pattern is worth memorizing on its own, since it appears repeatedly in scenario questions asking how one event can independently drive multiple downstream systems.

concepts.heading: Lambda Scaling and Packaging Recap
concepts.body: Lambda questions in this domain cluster around two axes: concurrency controls (reserved concurrency to cap and guarantee capacity, provisioned concurrency to eliminate cold starts) and packaging choices (Layers to share dependencies, .zip versus container images for size limits), plus the versions-and-aliases model that underlies canary and linear deployments. Event source mappings for SQS, DynamoDB Streams, and Kinesis, along with DLQs for isolating poison messages, round out the operational side of Lambda that this exam tests heavily.

concepts.heading: Data Store Selection Recap
concepts.body: The data store material spans DynamoDB (key design, GSI vs LSI, transactions, DAX), relational options (RDS/Aurora and the Data API), S3 developer patterns (multipart upload, presigned URLs, event notifications), and in-memory stores (ElastiCache as a cache versus MemoryDB as a durable primary store). Because this domain carries 32% of the exam, the single highest-value study habit is being able to instantly map a described access pattern or consistency requirement to the correct store and the correct DynamoDB indexing choice.

concepts.heading: API and Integration Layer Recap
concepts.body: Rounding out the domain, API Gateway's integration types, caching, throttling, and Usage Plans control how clients reach backend compute, while AppSync's GraphQL model and Kinesis Data Streams handle more specialized needs: flexible multi-source querying with real-time subscriptions, and high-throughput ordered streams that multiple independent consumers can each replay. A scenario mentioning over-fetching, under-fetching, or multiple independent stream consumers is testing this specific pair rather than the core REST/Lambda material.

examPoints: When a scenario states or implies whether communication is synchronous or asynchronous, and whether one consumer or many independent consumers need the data, the correct messaging service (SQS, SNS, or EventBridge) becomes clear almost immediately.

When a scenario describes a client that must fetch fields from several data sources in one request, or a stream that multiple independent applications must each replay, look to AppSync/GraphQL and Kinesis Data Streams respectively rather than a plain REST API or SQS.

quiz.q: Which pattern lets a single business event independently trigger processing in multiple unrelated downstream systems, none of which are affected by the others' failures?
choices: A single shared SQS queue
An SNS topic fanning out to one SQS queue per consumer
A synchronous chain of REST API calls
A single Lambda function calling each system in sequence
quiz.explain: The SNS-to-multiple-SQS fan-out pattern is the standard solution for independent, decoupled multi-consumer processing of one event.

quiz.q: Which Lambda configuration eliminates cold-start latency by keeping execution environments pre-warmed ahead of traffic?
choices: Reserved concurrency
Provisioned concurrency
Environment variable encryption
A dead-letter queue
quiz.explain: Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes execution environments so invocations skip the cold-start path; reserved concurrency only sets a concurrency ceiling and guarantee, without pre-warming anything.

days.recap: Domain 1 wrap-up: three messaging patterns (SQS/SNS/EventBridge), two Lambda concurrency controls, and DynamoDB's index/transaction choices are the highest-frequency topics to have cold before moving on.

days.title: Authentication and Authorization with Cognito and IAM

concepts.heading: Cognito User Pools and JWT Tokens
concepts.body: Amazon Cognito User Pools act as a managed identity provider for your application's end users, handling sign-up, sign-in, password policies, and multi-factor authentication, and issuing three JSON Web Tokens on successful login: an ID token describing the user's identity claims, an access token scoped for calling APIs, and a refresh token for obtaining new tokens without re-authenticating. These tokens are signed and time-limited, and any service that trusts the User Pool's public signing key can verify them without calling Cognito on every request.

concepts.heading: Wiring Cognito into API Gateway
concepts.body: API Gateway's Cognito authorizer type validates an incoming JWT against a specified User Pool automatically, rejecting requests with missing, expired, or invalid tokens before they ever reach your backend integration, and it can expose validated claims (like the user's sub or custom attributes) to your Lambda function through the request context. This is the standard, lowest-effort way to require end-user authentication on an API and should be the default choice whenever a scenario simply says 'only logged-in users' rather than describing a custom or federated identity scheme.

concepts.heading: Lambda Authorizers for Custom Logic
concepts.body: When authentication doesn't fit Cognito's model, such as validating a third-party OAuth token, a custom API key scheme, or a proprietary token format, API Gateway's Lambda authorizer (token-based or request-based) lets you run arbitrary code to produce an IAM policy document that allows or denies the request, optionally with a cached result for a configurable TTL to avoid invoking the authorizer on every single call. Lambda authorizers trade the simplicity of the Cognito authorizer for full flexibility, which is exactly why exam scenarios describing non-standard authentication schemes point here instead.

concepts.heading: Lambda Execution Roles and Least Privilege
concepts.body: Every Lambda function runs under an IAM execution role that governs what other AWS resources and actions it may call, and best practice is to scope this role down to only the specific actions and resource ARNs the function actually needs (for example, dynamodb:GetItem on one specific table) rather than granting broad service-level access. This principle of least privilege limits the blast radius if a function is ever compromised or misconfigured, and it is one of the most heavily emphasized security practices across the entire exam, not just this domain.

concepts.heading: IAM Policy Condition Keys
concepts.body: IAM policies can include a Condition block that restricts when a permission applies, based on keys like aws:SourceIp (limit access to a CIDR range), aws:RequestedRegion, aws:SecureTransport (require HTTPS), or resource tags via aws:ResourceTag, allowing fine-grained, context-aware access control beyond a simple allow/deny on an action and resource. This is commonly combined with resource tagging strategies so that access can be scoped dynamically (for example, 'only allow access to resources tagged with the caller's department') without maintaining a separate policy per team.

examPoints: A scenario stating that only end users who have signed in through the application's own login screen should be able to call an API is pointing to an API Gateway Cognito authorizer, the simplest managed solution for that exact requirement.

A scenario describing a non-standard or third-party authentication scheme (custom tokens, an external OAuth provider not backed by a User Pool) is pointing to a Lambda authorizer, since it is the only API Gateway authorizer type that runs fully custom logic.

quiz.q: An API should reject any request that does not include a valid, unexpired token issued by the application's own Cognito User Pool, before the request reaches the backend Lambda function. What should be configured?
choices: A Lambda authorizer that manually re-implements JWT validation
An API Gateway Cognito authorizer attached to the User Pool
An IAM resource policy on the Lambda function
A WAF rate-based rule
quiz.explain: The built-in Cognito authorizer validates User Pool JWTs automatically without any custom code; a Lambda authorizer (choice A) could do this too but would require reimplementing logic the Cognito authorizer already provides for free.

quiz.q: A Lambda function should be limited to reading and writing only one specific DynamoDB table, and nothing else, in order to minimize the impact of any future misconfiguration. What should be done?
choices: Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the function's execution role
Scope the function's execution role to only the required DynamoDB actions on that table's specific ARN
Use the account root credentials in the function code
Grant access to all DynamoDB tables to simplify future changes
quiz.explain: Scoping the execution role to the minimum required actions and resource ARN follows the least privilege principle; attaching AdministratorAccess (choice A) is the opposite of least privilege and a common wrong-answer trap.

days.recap: Cognito User Pools issue JWTs that an API Gateway Cognito authorizer validates automatically, Lambda authorizers handle custom or third-party auth schemes, execution roles should follow least privilege, and IAM condition keys add fine-grained, context-aware restrictions.

days.title: STS Temporary Credentials and Service-to-Service Authentication

concepts.heading: AssumeRole and Temporary Credentials
concepts.body: The AWS Security Token Service (STS) AssumeRole API lets application code exchange its current identity for a short-lived set of temporary credentials (an access key, secret key, and session token, typically valid from 15 minutes to 12 hours) tied to a different IAM role, which is how you grant cross-account access or scoped-down access without ever distributing long-lived access keys. Because the credentials expire automatically and cannot be reused after that, a leaked temporary credential is a far smaller risk than a leaked long-term access key, which is one reason AWS recommends AssumeRole-based patterns wherever they fit.

concepts.heading: Resource-Based Policies
concepts.body: Unlike identity-based policies (attached to a user or role, defining what that identity can do), a resource-based policy is attached directly to the resource itself, such as an S3 bucket policy or a Lambda function's resource policy, and it defines who (which principal, potentially in another AWS account) is allowed to access that resource. Resource-based policies are the only mechanism for granting cross-account access to some resource types without the calling account needing to assume a role in the resource's account first, and both the identity-based and resource-based policies are evaluated together when AWS determines whether to allow a request.

concepts.heading: Service Roles for AWS-to-AWS Calls
concepts.body: When one AWS service needs to invoke another on your behalf, such as EventBridge invoking a Lambda function or S3 delivering an event notification to an SQS queue, the target resource typically needs a resource-based policy explicitly permitting that calling service (as a principal) to invoke it; console-driven setup in EventBridge or S3 usually adds this automatically, but Infrastructure-as-Code deployments frequently miss it, making 'my trigger isn't firing' a very common real-world and exam scenario traced back to a missing resource-based permission.

concepts.heading: OIDC Federation for CI/CD Pipelines
concepts.body: Rather than storing long-lived AWS access keys as secrets in a CI/CD platform like GitHub Actions, OIDC federation lets the CI/CD provider present a signed OIDC token to AWS STS, which validates it against a configured IAM identity provider and issues short-lived temporary credentials tied to an IAM role, with no long-term secret ever stored in the pipeline configuration. This has become the recommended modern pattern for deployment pipelines specifically because it eliminates the risk of an exfiltrated long-lived key, and the trust relationship can be scoped down to a specific GitHub repository and branch using condition keys in the role's trust policy.

concepts.heading: Cross-Account Access Patterns
concepts.body: A common multi-account pattern combines these ideas: an application in Account A assumes a role in Account B (via STS AssumeRole), and that role in Account B is only assumable because its trust policy explicitly lists Account A's role ARN as a trusted principal, creating a two-sided handshake where both the trusting and the trusted side must agree. This pattern underlies AWS Organizations cross-account automation, third-party SaaS tools that need read access into your account, and cross-account CI/CD deployment roles alike.

examPoints: A scenario describing a CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions or similar) that should deploy to AWS without storing a long-lived access key anywhere in the pipeline's configuration is pointing to OIDC federation combined with an assumable IAM role.

A scenario where an EventBridge rule or S3 event notification is supposed to trigger a Lambda function or queue but nothing happens is pointing to a missing resource-based policy statement on the target granting the calling service permission to invoke it.

quiz.q: A team wants their GitHub Actions pipeline to deploy to AWS without ever storing a long-lived AWS access key as a GitHub secret. What is the recommended approach?
choices: Store an IAM user's access key and secret key as encrypted GitHub secrets
Configure OIDC federation so GitHub Actions assumes an IAM role via STS for short-lived credentials
Use the AWS account's root credentials
Embed the credentials directly in the pipeline YAML file
quiz.explain: OIDC federation issues short-lived, automatically expiring credentials with no long-term secret to leak; storing an access key as a secret (choice A) still leaves a long-lived credential that could be exfiltrated.

quiz.q: An EventBridge rule is configured to invoke a target Lambda function, but the function is never triggered even though the rule shows as enabled. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The Lambda function has too much memory allocated
The Lambda function's resource-based policy does not grant EventBridge permission to invoke it
The DynamoDB table used by the function does not exist
The API Gateway stage was not deployed
quiz.explain: Cross-service invocation generally requires the target's resource-based policy to explicitly permit the calling service as a principal; without it, the invocation is silently denied at the permissions layer.

days.recap: STS AssumeRole grants short-lived credentials instead of long-term keys, resource-based policies define who may access a resource including cross-account principals, service-to-service calls need matching resource-based permissions, and OIDC federation removes long-lived secrets from CI/CD pipelines.

days.title: Implementing Encryption with KMS and Envelope Encryption

concepts.heading: Client-Side Encryption with the AWS Encryption SDK
concepts.body: The AWS Encryption SDK is a client-side library that implements envelope encryption for you: it asks KMS for a data key, uses that data key to encrypt your plaintext locally, and packages the resulting ciphertext together with the encrypted (not plaintext) copy of the data key into a single message format your application can store or transmit. This is the standard tool when application code itself must perform encryption, rather than relying on an AWS service to encrypt data automatically at rest.

concepts.heading: Server-Side vs Client-Side Encryption
concepts.body: Server-side encryption (SSE), such as S3's SSE-KMS or SSE-S3, is applied automatically by the AWS service at the moment data is written to durable storage, meaning the plaintext does briefly exist within the AWS service boundary during the request. Client-side encryption instead encrypts the data before it ever leaves your application, so AWS never sees the plaintext at all, which is the differentiator that regulated industries (finance, healthcare) often require for their most sensitive data categories even though it adds engineering complexity that server-side encryption avoids.

concepts.heading: The GenerateDataKey API and Envelope Encryption
concepts.body: KMS's GenerateDataKey API returns two things in one call: a plaintext data key and that same key encrypted under a specified KMS key (the Customer Master Key). The calling application uses the plaintext key to encrypt its data immediately and then deliberately discards the plaintext key from memory, retaining only the encrypted copy alongside the ciphertext; decryption later calls KMS's Decrypt API with the encrypted key to recover the plaintext key just long enough to decrypt the data. This 'envelope' approach means large volumes of data never need to be sent to KMS directly (KMS only ever handles the small data key), which is both faster and how KMS supports encrypting arbitrarily large objects despite KMS's own API having small payload limits.

concepts.heading: KMS Key Policies vs IAM Policies
concepts.body: Every KMS key has its own resource-based key policy that is evaluated in addition to, not instead of, IAM identity-based policies, and by default a newly created KMS key's policy only grants the account root full access; other principals get no access to the key at all unless the key policy explicitly grants it, or the key policy delegates permission management to IAM policies (which many console-created keys do by default). This means an IAM policy granting kms:Decrypt to a role is not sufficient on its own if the key's own policy does not also allow that principal, which is a frequently tested gotcha and a common source of confusing 'access denied' errors in practice.

concepts.heading: Key Rotation and Grants
concepts.body: AWS-managed KMS keys rotate automatically every year, and customer-managed KMS keys can have automatic annual rotation enabled as well, with KMS transparently retaining old key material so that data encrypted under a previous key version can still be decrypted after rotation. KMS grants provide a more temporary, programmatic way to delegate specific key permissions (such as to a particular Lambda function) without editing the key policy directly, and grants can be created and revoked far more dynamically than policy edits, which suits automated systems provisioning access on the fly.

examPoints: A scenario describing a regulatory requirement that data must be encrypted by the application itself before it is ever transmitted to AWS is pointing to client-side encryption via the AWS Encryption SDK, not to an AWS service's server-side encryption feature.

A scenario where an IAM policy already allows kms:Decrypt for a role, but the role still cannot use the key, is pointing to the KMS key's own resource-based key policy needing to explicitly allow that principal as well.

quiz.q: A financial services application must encrypt sensitive records before they ever leave the application server, such that AWS never has access to the plaintext at any point. What approach satisfies this?
choices: Enable S3 default encryption with SSE-S3
Use the AWS Encryption SDK to perform client-side envelope encryption before uploading
Enable SSE-KMS on the destination S3 bucket
Store the data unencrypted and rely on bucket policies for protection
quiz.explain: Client-side encryption with the AWS Encryption SDK ensures plaintext never leaves the application; both SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS (choices A and C) are server-side options where AWS handles the plaintext during the write.

quiz.q: A developer's IAM role has an identity-based policy explicitly allowing kms:Decrypt, yet calls to decrypt using a specific customer-managed KMS key are still denied. What should be checked first?
choices: Whether the developer's password meets complexity requirements
Whether the KMS key's own key policy also grants that principal permission
Whether the S3 bucket has versioning enabled
Whether the VPC has a NAT gateway
quiz.explain: KMS evaluates both the identity-based IAM policy and the resource-based key policy, and access is denied unless both allow it; an IAM Allow alone is not sufficient if the key policy does not also permit that principal.

days.recap: The Encryption SDK implements client-side envelope encryption while SSE happens automatically server-side, GenerateDataKey returns a plaintext-and-encrypted key pair so only the small key touches KMS, and KMS evaluates both key policy and IAM policy together before granting access.

days.title: Certificate Management and Web Application Protection with ACM and WAF

concepts.heading: AWS Certificate Manager for TLS
concepts.body: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) issues and automatically renews public SSL/TLS certificates at no additional cost, provided the certificate is used with an integrated AWS service such as API Gateway, CloudFront, or an Application Load Balancer, and it handles domain validation through DNS (adding a CNAME record) or email. Because renewal is automatic as long as the validation record remains in place, ACM eliminates the operational burden and outage risk of manually tracking certificate expiration dates that plagued pre-cloud TLS management.

concepts.heading: Regional Requirements for Custom Domains
concepts.body: When attaching an ACM certificate to an API Gateway custom domain, the certificate's required region depends on the endpoint type: edge-optimized custom domains (which use CloudFront under the hood) require the certificate to be requested in us-east-1 regardless of which region the API itself runs in, while regional custom domains require the certificate to be requested in that same region as the API. Requesting the certificate in the wrong region is one of the most common real-world setup mistakes and shows up as a certificate that simply does not appear as selectable when configuring the custom domain.

concepts.heading: AWS WAF for Layer 7 Protection
concepts.body: AWS WAF is a web application firewall that inspects HTTP(S) requests before they reach API Gateway, CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer, or AppSync, and can block requests matching rules for SQL injection, cross-site scripting, known bad IP reputation lists, geographic restrictions, or custom conditions on headers and body content. WAF rules are grouped into Web ACLs, which can combine AWS Managed Rule groups (maintained by AWS or AWS Marketplace sellers) with your own custom rules, and WAF operates purely at the application layer, complementing (not replacing) network-layer protections like security groups.

concepts.heading: Rate-Based Rules for Abuse Mitigation
concepts.body: A WAF rate-based rule automatically counts requests from each individual IP address over a rolling five-minute window and blocks (or challenges) any IP that exceeds a configured threshold, which is the standard mitigation for application-layer scenarios like credential-stuffing login attempts or a single misbehaving client hammering an endpoint, as opposed to a large-scale distributed volumetric attack, which AWS Shield addresses at the network layer instead. Rate-based rules can be scoped to only specific URI paths, such as protecting just a login endpoint rather than throttling the entire application.

concepts.heading: Combining ACM and WAF in a Request Path
concepts.body: In a typical public API design, ACM provides the TLS certificate terminating HTTPS at CloudFront or the API Gateway custom domain, and WAF is attached to that same CloudFront distribution or API Gateway stage to inspect and filter requests before they are decrypted content reaches your backend logic; because WAF sits in front of the entry point rather than inside the application, malicious requests are blocked before consuming any Lambda invocations or database queries, which also has a direct cost benefit at scale.

examPoints: A scenario asking for a free, automatically renewing TLS certificate for an API Gateway custom domain or CloudFront distribution is pointing to AWS Certificate Manager rather than a manually purchased and installed certificate.

A scenario describing repeated login attempts or abusive request volume from a small number of specific IP addresses is pointing to a WAF rate-based rule, which is designed to detect and block exactly that per-IP pattern.

quiz.q: A team needs a TLS certificate for a new API Gateway edge-optimized custom domain and wants renewal to happen automatically with no ongoing manual work. What should they do, and in which region should the certificate be requested?
choices: Purchase a certificate from a third-party CA and upload it manually every year
Request a free ACM certificate in us-east-1, since edge-optimized custom domains use CloudFront
Request a free ACM certificate in the API's own region
Use a self-signed certificate to avoid third-party costs
quiz.explain: Edge-optimized API Gateway custom domains are backed by CloudFront, which requires ACM certificates to be requested in us-east-1 regardless of the API's actual region; requesting it in the API's own region (choice C) is the correct approach only for regional custom domains.

quiz.q: Security logs show a small number of IP addresses making an abnormally high volume of login requests within short time windows. What AWS WAF feature directly addresses this?
choices: A geographic match rule blocking entire countries
A rate-based rule scoped to the login endpoint
Disabling WAF logging to reduce noise
An ACM certificate renewal
quiz.explain: A rate-based rule automatically tracks per-IP request counts and blocks IPs that exceed the threshold, which precisely matches this credential-stuffing-style pattern; a geographic rule (choice A) would be both too broad and not targeted at the actual abuse pattern described.

days.recap: ACM issues and auto-renews free TLS certificates but requires the right region for edge-optimized versus regional custom domains, and WAF blocks Layer 7 attacks with managed and custom rules, including rate-based rules for per-IP abuse mitigation.

days.title: Managing Secrets: Secrets Manager and Parameter Store

concepts.heading: Secrets Manager and Automatic Rotation
concepts.body: AWS Secrets Manager stores secrets such as database credentials and API keys as encrypted values and, uniquely among AWS's secret storage options, supports automatic rotation on a schedule using a Lambda rotation function that Secrets Manager invokes to generate a new credential, update it in the target data store (like updating an RDS master password), and then update the stored secret value, all without any application downtime if the application always fetches the current secret at connection time. AWS provides built-in rotation function templates for RDS, Aurora, Redshift, and DocumentDB, which removes most of the custom code burden for the common case.

concepts.heading: Parameter Store for Cost-Effective Configuration
concepts.body: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store stores both plain configuration values (String and StringList types) and encrypted secrets (SecureString type, encrypted via KMS) in a hierarchical namespace, and its standard tier is free, making it the more cost-effective choice for configuration values and secrets that do not require automatic rotation. Parameter Store lacks Secrets Manager's built-in rotation scheduling (rotation would need to be built manually via EventBridge and a custom Lambda function), so the deciding factor between the two services is almost always whether automatic rotation is a hard requirement.

concepts.heading: Caching Secrets to Reduce Latency and Cost
concepts.body: Because retrieving a secret from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store on every single function invocation adds latency and API call cost, and because both services enforce request rate limits, the recommended pattern is to fetch the secret once and cache it in memory for a short time-to-live using either the official AWS Secrets Manager caching client libraries (available for several languages) or a simple global-scope variable in a Lambda function that persists across warm invocations. This caching pattern must still account for rotation: a cached credential can become stale if it is not refreshed shortly after a rotation event.

concepts.heading: Avoiding Hardcoded Secrets in Source Code
concepts.body: Hardcoding credentials directly in application source code is one of the most common and most exam-tested security anti-patterns, because it exposes the secret to anyone with source access, gets committed permanently into version control history even if later removed, and cannot be rotated without a code deployment. Static analysis tools integrated into CI pipelines (including AWS's own tools and third-party options) can scan commits for patterns resembling access keys or credentials and block a merge before the secret ever reaches a shared branch.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between Secrets Manager and Parameter Store in Practice
concepts.body: A practical rule of thumb: use Secrets Manager for anything that represents live database or service credentials that should rotate periodically, and use Parameter Store for feature flags, non-sensitive configuration, and secrets you're willing to rotate manually or infrequently, since Parameter Store's advanced tier does add some Secrets-Manager-like capabilities (larger parameter size, higher throughput) for an additional cost if a team wants to standardize on one service.

examPoints: A scenario requiring a database password to rotate automatically on a schedule with zero application downtime is pointing to Secrets Manager's built-in rotation feature, not Parameter Store, which has no native rotation scheduler.

A scenario describing a simple, rarely changing configuration value (like a feature flag) where minimizing cost matters is pointing to Parameter Store's free standard tier rather than Secrets Manager.

quiz.q: A company wants its RDS master password to rotate automatically every 30 days, with the application always able to fetch the current value without any planned downtime. Which service and feature should be used?
choices: Parameter Store SecureString with manual updates
Secrets Manager with automatic rotation configured
Plain-text environment variables updated by hand
Hardcoding the password and redeploying monthly
quiz.explain: Secrets Manager's built-in automatic rotation, using an AWS-provided Lambda rotation template for RDS, is purpose-built for exactly this requirement; Parameter Store (choice A) has no native scheduled rotation mechanism.

quiz.q: A team needs to store a simple, infrequently changing feature flag value and wants to minimize ongoing cost. Which option is most appropriate?
choices: AWS Secrets Manager
Systems Manager Parameter Store standard tier
AWS Certificate Manager
AWS WAF
quiz.explain: Parameter Store's standard tier is free and well suited to simple configuration values that don't need automatic rotation; Secrets Manager (choice A) incurs per-secret and per-API-call costs that aren't justified for a plain feature flag.
