days.recap: Secrets Manager adds automatic, scheduled rotation for live credentials, Parameter Store is a cheaper option for configuration and secrets that rotate manually or not at all, and both should be cached briefly in application memory and never hardcoded into source code.

days.title: Protecting Sensitive Data: Safe Logging and Least Privilege

concepts.heading: Preventing Sensitive Data in Logs
concepts.body: Application code must actively avoid writing passwords, full card numbers, or other personally identifiable information into log statements, since logs are often retained for long periods, exported to third-party tools, and accessible to a broader set of engineers than the production database itself. CloudWatch Logs data protection policies can automatically detect and mask common sensitive data patterns (like credit card numbers or AWS credentials) as logs are ingested, providing a safety net for the cases where application-level masking is missed, but they are a backstop, not a substitute for careful logging discipline in the code itself.

concepts.heading: Avoiding Information Disclosure in Error Responses
concepts.body: Detailed stack traces, internal file paths, or database error messages returned directly in an API's error response give an attacker a roadmap of the system's internals and should instead be logged internally (where the operations team can see them) while the client receives a generic, non-revealing error message and a correlation ID they can reference when reporting the issue. This separation between what is logged for debugging and what is returned to the caller is a core secure-coding practice tested throughout this domain.

concepts.heading: Enforcing Least Privilege in IAM Policies
concepts.body: The least privilege principle means granting only the specific actions and resource ARNs a principal actually needs, and it applies equally to human IAM users and to Lambda execution roles or EC2 instance profiles; a policy using Action: "*" or Resource: "*" is a red flag because it grants far more than almost any real workload requires and dramatically increases the blast radius of a compromised credential or a coding mistake. IAM Access Analyzer's policy generation feature can even observe a role's actual CloudTrail activity over a period of time and generate a tightly scoped policy based on what was genuinely used.

concepts.heading: IAM Access Analyzer for Unused Permission Discovery
concepts.body: Beyond generating scoped-down policies, IAM Access Analyzer continuously analyzes policies attached across an account or organization to flag resources that are shared with external entities (unexpected cross-account or public access) and to identify permissions that have gone unused over a lookback period, giving security teams a concrete, evidence-based list of access to revoke rather than relying on manual policy review. This turns least-privilege enforcement into an ongoing, iterative process rather than a one-time exercise done only at design time.

concepts.heading: Encrypting and Restricting Access to Log Data Itself
concepts.body: CloudWatch Log groups can be encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key and access to reading them controlled through IAM policies scoped to specific log group ARNs, ensuring that even internally, only engineers or services with an actual need can read potentially sensitive operational logs, which closes the loop between 'don't log sensitive data' and 'restrict who can read the logs that remain.'

examPoints: A scenario describing sensitive data such as credit card numbers appearing in plaintext in application logs is pointing to fixing the logging code to mask that data before it is written, with CloudWatch Logs data protection policies as an additional safety net.

A scenario showing an IAM policy with an Action of "*" or a Resource of "*" is almost always testing whether you recognize this as a least-privilege violation that should be scoped down to the specific actions and resources actually required.

quiz.q: A security review discovers that customer credit card numbers are being written in plaintext to application logs. What should be done first?
choices: Extend the CloudWatch Logs retention period
Modify the application to mask or omit sensitive data before logging, and consider a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy as a backstop
Disable CloudWatch Logs entirely
Delete the affected log group
quiz.explain: The root cause is that sensitive data is being logged in the first place, so the fix belongs in the application's logging code, with a data protection policy as an additional safeguard; deleting the log group (choice D) does not prevent the problem from recurring.

quiz.q: An IAM policy attached to a Lambda execution role uses "Action": "*" and "Resource": "*". Why is this a problem?
choices: It makes the function run more slowly
It violates least privilege by granting far more access than the function likely needs
It prevents the function from being encrypted
It disables CloudWatch Logs for the function
quiz.explain: A wildcard action and resource grants sweeping permissions well beyond what most workloads require, directly violating least privilege and increasing the impact of any compromise; it has no direct effect on function performance, encryption, or logging (choices A, C, D).

days.recap: Sensitive data should be masked before it is ever logged, error responses should hide internal details from callers, IAM policies should follow least privilege rather than using wildcards, and Access Analyzer helps generate and continuously validate scoped-down policies.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Security

concepts.heading: Authentication Layer Recap
concepts.body: This domain draws a clear line between end-user authentication, handled by Cognito User Pools and API Gateway's Cognito or Lambda authorizers, and service-to-service or cross-account authentication, handled by STS AssumeRole, resource-based policies, and OIDC federation for CI/CD. Recognizing which side of that line a scenario is describing is usually the fastest way to eliminate two of the four answer choices immediately.

concepts.heading: Encryption and Data Protection Recap
concepts.body: The encryption material centers on the distinction between server-side encryption (automatic, applied by the AWS service) and client-side encryption via the AWS Encryption SDK (manual, application-controlled envelope encryption using KMS's GenerateDataKey), plus the critical detail that KMS evaluates both key policies and IAM policies together. ACM and WAF add TLS certificate management and Layer 7 application protection, respectively, rounding out the 'protect data in transit and at rest' half of this domain.

concepts.heading: Secrets and Least Privilege Recap
concepts.body: Secrets Manager (automatic rotation) versus Parameter Store (cheaper, manual rotation) is a frequently tested pair, alongside the broader theme of least privilege that spans IAM policy design, safe logging practices, and IAM Access Analyzer's ability to detect unused permissions and cross-account exposure.

concepts.heading: Domain 2's Recurring Question Pattern
concepts.body: Across nearly every Domain 2 scenario, the exam is really asking one of three things: who or what is allowed to do this, is the data adequately protected at rest and in transit, or is a secret or certificate being managed safely rather than hardcoded or left to expire. Sorting a scenario into one of these three buckets before reading the answer choices is usually enough to eliminate half of them immediately, since the wrong answers typically address a different bucket entirely.

examPoints: Before selecting an answer, decide whether the scenario is about authenticating an end user, authenticating one service or account to another, or protecting data at rest or in transit — each maps to a distinct cluster of services in this domain.

A wrong-answer choice in this domain frequently describes a real AWS service used for the wrong job, such as suggesting Parameter Store when automatic rotation is required, so eliminate choices that solve an adjacent but different problem before picking the best remaining option.

quiz.q: Which API Gateway authorizer type is the standard, lowest-effort choice for validating that a caller is logged in through the application's own Cognito User Pool?
choices: IAM authorization only
Cognito authorizer
A VPC endpoint policy
A NAT Gateway route
quiz.explain: The Cognito authorizer validates User Pool JWTs automatically with no custom code required.

quiz.q: Which service should be used to automatically rotate an RDS database credential on a schedule?
choices: Systems Manager Parameter Store
AWS Secrets Manager
AWS Certificate Manager
AWS WAF
quiz.explain: Secrets Manager provides built-in scheduled rotation using Lambda rotation functions, including AWS-provided templates for RDS.

days.recap: Domain 2 wrap-up: Cognito handles end-user auth, STS/resource policies/OIDC handle service and pipeline auth, KMS/ACM/WAF protect data and traffic, and Secrets Manager versus Parameter Store comes down to whether rotation is required.

days.title: Preparing Deployment Artifacts: Lambda Packaging and Container Images

concepts.heading: Zip Deployment Packages and Their Limits
concepts.body: A Lambda .zip deployment package bundles your handler code and its dependencies, subject to a 50MB compressed size limit for direct upload and a 250MB unzipped size limit (shared with any attached Layers), which is usually sufficient for typical application code but becomes a hard constraint for functions bundling large machine learning libraries, native binaries, or extensive dependency trees. When a function approaches these limits, the two standard remedies are trimming dependencies (removing unused files, using lighter alternative libraries) or moving to Layers to separate shared dependencies, before resorting to a container image.

concepts.heading: Container Image Deployment for Large Dependencies
concepts.body: Lambda also supports deploying a function as a container image up to 10GB, stored in Amazon ECR, which is the clear choice once a function's dependencies genuinely exceed the .zip package limits, such as bundling a large ML inference library or a sizable native toolchain. A Lambda-compatible container image must include the Lambda Runtime Interface Client, which implements the API contract Lambda uses to invoke the function inside the container, and AWS publishes base images for each supported runtime that already include this client so teams don't need to implement it themselves.

concepts.heading: Optimizing Package Size for Faster Cold Starts
concepts.body: Regardless of packaging format, smaller deployment artifacts generally cold-start faster, since Lambda must download and extract the package (or pull the container image layers) before initializing the runtime; common optimizations include excluding test files and documentation from the package, using Layers to avoid duplicating shared dependencies across functions, and tree-shaking or bundling tools (like esbuild for Node.js) that strip unused code paths out of the final artifact. For container images, structuring the Dockerfile so that frequently changing application code sits in the last layer (while rarely changing dependencies sit in earlier, cached layers) also speeds up build and deployment time, though it does not materially affect cold-start latency once deployed.

concepts.heading: Amazon ECR as the Container Registry
concepts.body: Amazon ECR is a fully managed, private-by-default Docker/OCI container registry tightly integrated with IAM for access control and with Lambda, ECS, and EKS for pulling images at deploy time, and it supports both mutable and immutable image tags depending on whether you want to allow a tag like 'latest' to be overwritten. ECR image scanning (basic, powered by Clair-derived open-source scanning, or enhanced, powered by Amazon Inspector) automatically checks stored images against known CVE databases and can be configured to scan on every push, giving teams visibility into vulnerable base images or dependencies before they are deployed.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between Zip and Container Deployment
concepts.body: The decision in practice, and on the exam, comes down to size and tooling familiarity: choose .zip packaging (optionally with Layers) for typical application code well under the size limits, and choose container images when dependencies are large, when a team already has a Docker-based build pipeline they want to reuse for Lambda, or when they need the ability to scan images with the same tooling used for their ECS/EKS containers.

examPoints: A scenario describing a Lambda function that must bundle a large machine learning library exceeding the 250MB unzipped .zip limit is pointing to container image deployment via ECR, since that format supports up to 10GB.
A scenario asking how to automatically detect known vulnerabilities in a container image before or as it is deployed is pointing to Amazon ECR's built-in image scanning feature.

quiz.q: A Lambda function needs to bundle a machine learning inference library whose unpacked size exceeds 250MB, well beyond the .zip deployment package limit. What should the team do?
choices: Force the .zip file to compress further and try again
Package the function as a container image stored in Amazon ECR
Split the library across many Lambda functions
Remove the library and reimplement its logic from scratch
quiz.explain: Container images support up to 10GB, comfortably accommodating large libraries that exceed .zip limits; further compression (choice A) does not change the unzipped size limit that actually applies.

quiz.q: A security team wants every container image pushed to the company's registry to be automatically checked against known CVEs before deployment. What should be enabled?
choices: AWS CodeGuru Profiler
Amazon ECR image scanning
AWS X-Ray tracing
CloudWatch Logs Insights
quiz.explain: ECR image scanning automatically checks stored container images for known vulnerabilities; the other options address performance profiling, distributed tracing, and log analysis, not vulnerability scanning.

days.recap: Lambda deployment packages come as .zip files (250MB unzipped limit) or container images (10GB, via ECR), large dependencies favor container images, package size affects cold-start time, and ECR image scanning catches known vulnerabilities automatically.

days.title: Infrastructure as Code for Serverless: SAM and CDK

concepts.heading: AWS SAM as a CloudFormation Extension
concepts.body: The AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM) extends CloudFormation with a small set of simplified resource types, like AWS::Serverless::Function and AWS::Serverless::Api, that expand into the much more verbose underlying CloudFormation resources at deployment time, letting you define a Lambda function, its API Gateway trigger, and an IAM role in a handful of lines of YAML instead of dozens. The SAM CLI wraps this with commands like sam build (resolving and packaging dependencies), sam deploy (creating or updating the CloudFormation stack), and sam local invoke (running a function locally).

concepts.heading: Local Testing with the SAM CLI
concepts.body: sam local invoke runs a single Lambda function inside a Docker container that emulates the real Lambda execution environment, letting a developer test a function's logic against a sample event file without any AWS deployment, and sam local start-api goes further by emulating an entire API Gateway plus Lambda backend locally so you can send real HTTP requests to routes defined in your SAM template during development. This tight local feedback loop is one of SAM's most valuable features for iterative serverless development, since deploying to AWS just to test a small code change is slow by comparison.

concepts.heading: AWS CDK: Infrastructure Defined in a Programming Language
concepts.body: The AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) lets you define infrastructure using TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, or Go, with the full expressive power of a real programming language, including loops, conditionals, functions, and classes, rather than a declarative templating language; running cdk synth compiles your code down into one or more standard CloudFormation templates, which CDK then deploys through CloudFormation exactly like a hand-written template would be. Because the actual deployment mechanism is still CloudFormation underneath, CDK inherits CloudFormation's stack, drift detection, and rollback behavior.

concepts.heading: Constructs and Reusability in CDK
concepts.body: CDK organizes infrastructure into Constructs, reusable building blocks ranging from low-level (a single CloudFormation resource, L1), to curated (a sensible default configuration of a resource with best practices baked in, L2), to high-level patterns (an entire multi-resource architecture like 'a Lambda function behind an API Gateway with a DynamoDB table', L3), which lets teams share and reuse well-tested infrastructure patterns as ordinary code packages the same way they'd share an application library. This composability is CDK's core advantage over SAM for larger, more complex infrastructure that has repeated patterns across many stacks or teams.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between SAM and CDK
concepts.body: SAM's simpler, purpose-built YAML syntax and first-class local-testing tooling make it a strong fit for straightforward serverless applications and teams that want minimal tooling overhead, while CDK's general-purpose programming language and construct-based reuse make it better suited for complex infrastructure with conditional logic, extensive resource reuse across projects, or teams that already prefer defining everything, application and infrastructure alike, in one language. Some teams even use CDK to define their infrastructure while still deploying serverless applications that internally follow SAM-like patterns, since the two are not mutually exclusive at an organizational level.

examPoints: A scenario asking for a simple, quick way to define a serverless application and test it locally before deploying is pointing to AWS SAM and its sam local commands.

A scenario describing complex conditional infrastructure logic, or a need to share reusable infrastructure patterns as versioned code across many teams, is pointing to AWS CDK and its Construct model.

quiz.q: A team wants to define a Lambda function and its API Gateway trigger in a concise template and test the API locally before deploying to AWS. What tool fits this best?
choices: Raw hand-written CloudFormation JSON
AWS SAM with the sam local CLI commands
Manual console configuration for every change
A general-purpose configuration management tool unrelated to AWS
quiz.explain: SAM's simplified resource types plus its local testing commands (sam local invoke, sam local start-api) are purpose-built for concise serverless definition and local iteration; raw CloudFormation (choice A) would require far more boilerplate to achieve the same result.

quiz.q: An infrastructure team needs to define complex, conditional infrastructure logic and share reusable multi-resource patterns as versioned packages across several application teams. What should they use?
choices: AWS SAM only
AWS CDK with custom Constructs
Manual console clicks repeated per environment
AWS CodeDeploy
quiz.explain: CDK's general-purpose language support and Construct model are designed exactly for expressing conditional logic and packaging reusable infrastructure; CodeDeploy (choice D) handles deployment strategies, not infrastructure definition.

days.recap: SAM offers concise, serverless-focused YAML with strong local-testing tooling, CDK offers a general-purpose programming language and reusable Constructs that synthesize to CloudFormation, and both ultimately deploy through CloudFormation.

days.title: CloudFormation Essentials: Templates, Stacks, and Change Sets

concepts.heading: Template Structure
concepts.body: A CloudFormation template is a JSON or YAML document organized into sections: Resources (the only required section, declaring the actual AWS resources to create), Parameters (input values supplied at deploy time, letting the same template be reused across environments), Outputs (values, like a created resource's ARN, that other stacks or humans can reference), Mappings (static lookup tables, often used for region-specific values), and Conditions (boolean logic controlling whether a resource is created based on parameter values). This declarative model means you describe the desired end state, and CloudFormation determines the sequence of API calls needed to reach it.

concepts.heading: Stacks and Deletion Behavior
concepts.body: A stack is the unit of management in CloudFormation: all the resources declared in one template deployment are tracked together, and deleting the stack by default deletes every resource it created, which is convenient for tearing down test environments but dangerous for anything holding important data unless you explicitly override that behavior. A resource's DeletionPolicy attribute can override the default, most commonly Retain (leave the resource, such as an S3 bucket or RDS instance, in place even after the stack is deleted) or Snapshot (for supported resources like RDS, take a final snapshot before deletion).

concepts.heading: Change Sets for Safe Updates
concepts.body: Before actually applying an update to a stack, you can generate a change set, which computes and displays exactly which resources will be added, modified, or replaced (and crucially, whether a 'modified' resource actually requires replacement, which would mean data loss for a stateful resource like a database) without making any changes yet. Reviewing a change set before executing it is the standard safeguard against an update unexpectedly triggering a disruptive resource replacement in a production environment, and it is considered a best practice step in any production deployment pipeline that uses CloudFormation.

concepts.heading: Nested Stacks for Modularity
concepts.body: A nested stack is a stack created as a resource within a parent template (using AWS::CloudFormation::Stack), which lets you factor out commonly repeated infrastructure, such as a standard VPC and security group setup, into a reusable child template that multiple parent stacks can reference, rather than copy-pasting the same resource declarations everywhere. Nested stacks are deployed and deleted together with their parent as a unit, which differs from fully independent sibling stacks that share values only through explicit cross-stack references.

concepts.heading: Cross-Stack References with Export and Fn::ImportValue
concepts.body: When two stacks are independent (not nested) but one needs a value the other created, such as a shared VPC ID, the producing stack declares an Output with an Export name, and the consuming stack's template uses Fn::ImportValue to reference that exported value at deploy time; CloudFormation will actually block deleting or modifying the exporting stack's exported output while another stack still imports it, which prevents accidentally breaking a dependent stack.

examPoints: A scenario expressing concern that an upcoming stack update might unexpectedly replace or delete a production resource is pointing to reviewing a change set before executing the update, since it previews exactly what will change.

A scenario describing multiple stacks needing to share a common resource value, such as a VPC ID created by one stack and consumed by another, is pointing to Export/Fn::ImportValue cross-stack references or, if the resources are meant to deploy together, a nested stack.

quiz.q: A team is about to update a production CloudFormation stack and is concerned the update might unintentionally replace a stateful resource, causing data loss. What should they do before applying the update?
choices: Apply the update immediately and monitor for issues afterward
Create and review a change set to see exactly what will be added, modified, or replaced
Delete the stack and recreate it from scratch
Disable termination protection on the stack
quiz.explain: A change set previews the precise impact of an update, including whether any resource requires replacement, before anything is actually changed; deleting and recreating the stack (choice C) is far more disruptive than the situation calls for.

quiz.q: Several CloudFormation stacks need to reuse the same VPC ID created by one central networking stack, without duplicating the VPC resource in every stack. What mechanism supports this?
choices: Copying the VPC ID manually into each template as a hardcoded value
Exporting the VPC ID as an Output in the networking stack and using Fn::ImportValue in the other stacks
Recreating the VPC independently in every stack
Using a DeletionPolicy of Retain on the VPC
quiz.explain: Export and Fn::ImportValue let one stack's output be safely referenced by other stacks without duplication; hardcoding the ID (choice A) would break the moment the VPC needed to be recreated or moved.

days.recap: Templates are organized into Resources, Parameters, Outputs, and more, stacks delete their resources by default unless a DeletionPolicy overrides that, change sets preview updates before they apply, and nested stacks or Export/ImportValue support modular reuse across stacks.

days.title: CI/CD Pipelines: CodePipeline, CodeBuild, and CodeArtifact

concepts.heading: CodePipeline Orchestration
concepts.body: AWS CodePipeline models a software release process as a series of stages (commonly Source, Build, Test, Deploy), each containing one or more actions that can run in parallel within a stage, with the pipeline automatically progressing to the next stage only if every action in the current stage succeeds, and stopping (with notifications available via EventBridge or SNS) if any action fails. Pipelines can pull source code from CodeCommit, GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, Bitbucket, or an S3 bucket, making CodePipeline source-agnostic even though it is a fully AWS-native orchestration service.

concepts.heading: Manual Approval Gates
concepts.body: CodePipeline supports a Manual Approval action type that pauses the pipeline at a specific stage until a designated person or group explicitly approves (or rejects) continuing, which is the standard mechanism for inserting human review before a production deployment while still keeping everything before that point (build, automated test) fully automated. Approval notifications can be routed through SNS to alert the right people the moment a pipeline is waiting on them.

concepts.heading: CodeBuild and buildspec.yml
concepts.body: AWS CodeBuild is a fully managed build service that runs commands defined in a buildspec.yml file, organized into phases: install (installing runtime dependencies), pre_build (steps like logging into a container registry), build (the actual compile or package step), and post_build (steps like running final tests or pushing build artifacts), with CodeBuild provisioning and tearing down the compute environment for each build automatically so you never manage build servers directly. CodeBuild scales horizontally to run multiple builds concurrently and supports custom Docker images for build environments with specialized toolchains.

concepts.heading: CodeArtifact for Dependency Management
concepts.body: AWS CodeArtifact is a managed artifact repository supporting common package formats (npm, PyPI, Maven, NuGet, and others) that lets an organization host private internal packages while also transparently proxying and caching packages from public upstream repositories like npmjs.com, so that a single configured repository endpoint serves both internal and public dependencies to build processes. This centralization improves both build reliability (a cached copy survives a public registry outage) and security (you can gate which upstream packages are allowed through).

concepts.heading: Failure Handling and Notifications Across the Pipeline
concepts.body: Any stage failure in CodePipeline halts progression to subsequent stages by default, which is what actually enforces that, for example, a failing automated test stage prevents a bad build from ever reaching a manual approval gate or production deployment; pipelines can be configured to send state-change notifications to EventBridge or SNS at any stage transition, which teams commonly wire into chat tools or paging systems so failures are noticed immediately rather than discovered later.

examPoints: A scenario requiring a human to explicitly review and approve a release before it reaches production, while keeping earlier build and test stages fully automated, is pointing to a CodePipeline Manual Approval action.
A scenario describing multiple teams needing to share and centrally manage internal npm, Maven, or PyPI packages, while also caching public dependencies, is pointing to AWS CodeArtifact.

quiz.q: A company wants every production deployment to require explicit sign-off from a release manager, while build and automated testing stages continue to run without any manual intervention. What should be added to the pipeline?
choices: A second CodeBuild project
A Manual Approval action placed before the production deployment stage
A CodeArtifact repository
A CloudFormation change set
quiz.explain: A Manual Approval action pauses the pipeline exactly at the point it's placed until a person approves, which is the built-in mechanism for this requirement; a second CodeBuild project (choice A) would not introduce any human review step.

quiz.q: Multiple engineering teams need a central, version-managed repository for internal npm packages, while also being able to pull public npm packages through the same endpoint. What service fits this need?
choices: Amazon S3 with manually zipped packages
AWS CodeArtifact
AWS CodeCommit
AWS CodeBuild
quiz.explain: CodeArtifact is purpose-built as a package repository supporting npm and other formats, including proxying public upstream registries; CodeCommit (choice C) is a source control service, not a package repository.

days.recap: CodePipeline orchestrates source-build-test-deploy stages and supports manual approval gates, CodeBuild runs buildspec.yml-defined phases in a managed build environment, and CodeArtifact centralizes internal and proxied public package dependencies.

days.title: CodeDeploy Deployment Strategies: In-Place, Blue/Green, Canary, and Linear

concepts.heading: In-Place Deployment
concepts.body: An in-place deployment updates the application directly on existing EC2 or on-premises instances, taking each instance (or a batch of instances) out of service, installing the new application version, and returning it to service, which requires no additional infrastructure but means capacity is temporarily reduced during the deployment and rollback is comparatively slow because it requires redeploying the previous version rather than simply switching traffic back.

concepts.heading: Blue/Green Deployment
concepts.body: A blue/green deployment provisions an entirely new, separate set of resources (the 'green' environment) running the new version alongside the existing 'blue' environment still serving live traffic, then shifts traffic over to green once it is verified healthy, keeping blue intact and ready as an instant rollback target if problems appear. CodeDeploy supports blue/green deployments for EC2/on-premises, ECS, and Lambda, though the mechanics differ: for EC2 it provisions new instances behind a load balancer, while for Lambda it works through alias traffic shifting rather than provisioning new compute.

concepts.heading: Lambda Deployment Configurations: Canary, Linear, and AllAtOnce
concepts.body: For Lambda specifically, CodeDeploy offers three traffic-shifting configurations defined in an AppSpec file: AllAtOnce shifts 100% of traffic to the new version immediately, Canary shifts a specified percentage (for example 10%) to the new version, waits a specified interval to observe results, and then shifts the remaining 90% all at once if no alarms fire, and Linear shifts traffic in equal increments at equal intervals (for example 10% every 2 minutes) until it reaches 100%, giving more gradual, continuous exposure than Canary's two-step jump.

concepts.heading: Automatic Rollback on CloudWatch Alarms
concepts.body: CodeDeploy can be configured to monitor one or more CloudWatch alarms during a deployment and automatically roll back to the previous version if any alarm enters an ALARM state, which is the standard way to make canary or linear deployments actually safe rather than just gradual, since a slow traffic shift only helps if something is actively watching for errors during that shift and can react faster than a human would. Without an alarm-triggered rollback configured, a bad deployment would still reach 100% of traffic once its timer completes, just more slowly than an AllAtOnce deployment would have.

concepts.heading: AppSpec Files and Deployment Groups
concepts.body: An AppSpec file (appspec.yml for EC2/on-premises, or a JSON/YAML structure referenced for Lambda and ECS) tells CodeDeploy what to deploy and, for EC2, defines lifecycle event hooks (like BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService) where you can run custom scripts at each stage of the deployment. A deployment group defines which instances, Auto Scaling group, or Lambda alias a given deployment configuration applies to, along with the associated alarms and rollback settings for that specific target.

examPoints: A scenario requiring automatic rollback to the previous Lambda version if error rates spike after a new version is deployed is pointing to configuring CodeDeploy with a CloudWatch alarm tied to automatic rollback, not merely picking a gradual deployment configuration alone.

A scenario emphasizing minimal downtime and the ability to instantly revert to the exact previous environment if something goes wrong is pointing to a blue/green deployment strategy rather than an in-place deployment.

quiz.q: After deploying a new Lambda version, the team wants CodeDeploy to automatically revert to the previous version if error rates spike, without requiring a person to notice and intervene manually. What should be configured?
choices: An AllAtOnce deployment configuration with no monitoring
A CloudWatch alarm attached to the deployment with automatic rollback enabled
A manual approval step in CodePipeline
A Lambda Layer update
quiz.explain: Automatic rollback triggered by a CloudWatch alarm is what makes a deployment self-healing without human intervention; a manual approval step (choice C) still requires a person to act, which contradicts the 'without requiring a person to notice' requirement.

quiz.q: A team wants to deploy a new application version to a completely separate environment, verify it, then shift traffic over with the ability to instantly revert to the untouched original environment if issues arise. Which deployment strategy is this?
choices: In-place deployment
Blue/green deployment
A single AllAtOnce Lambda shift with no alarms
Manually SSH-ing into each server
quiz.explain: Blue/green deployment provisions a separate environment for the new version and keeps the original environment intact as an instant rollback target, which is exactly what's described; in-place deployment (choice A) updates existing instances directly and cannot offer an instant revert to an untouched environment.

days.recap: In-place deployments update existing instances directly and roll back slowly, blue/green deployments switch traffic to a separate environment for instant rollback, Lambda supports Canary/Linear/AllAtOnce traffic shifting, and CloudWatch alarms make rollback automatic rather than just gradual.

days.title: Automating Development and Deployment Testing

concepts.heading: Fast Local Iteration with sam local invoke
concepts.body: sam local invoke lets a developer run a single Lambda function inside a Docker container that closely emulates the real Lambda execution environment, feeding it a sample event JSON file and immediately seeing the function's output and logs, all without deploying anything to AWS. This dramatically shortens the feedback loop during active development compared to redeploying to AWS for every small code change, and it works entirely offline once the required container images are pulled.

concepts.heading: Where Unit Tests and Integration Tests Belong in a Pipeline
concepts.body: Unit tests, which exercise isolated pieces of application logic without calling real AWS services, typically run during the CodeBuild build phase as part of building the deployment artifact, failing the pipeline immediately (and cheaply) if application logic is broken before any AWS resources are even touched. Integration tests, which validate real interactions between deployed components (an API endpoint actually calling a real Lambda function backed by a real DynamoDB table), can only meaningfully run after deployment to a staging environment, since they need real infrastructure to exercise.

concepts.heading: A Typical Automated Testing Pipeline Sequence
concepts.body: A mature serverless CI/CD pipeline typically sequences as: unit tests during the build phase, deployment to a staging environment, automated integration or end-to-end tests against that staging deployment, an optional manual approval gate, and finally deployment to production, with a failure at any stage halting progression to the next one. This ordering ensures that increasingly expensive and slow validation steps (integration and end-to-end tests) only run against code that has already passed the cheaper, faster unit test suite.

concepts.heading: Using X-Ray Locally for Pre-Deployment Performance Insight
concepts.body: The X-Ray SDK can be integrated into local testing (including with sam local invoke in some configurations) to capture timing information for external calls a function makes even before it's deployed, giving developers an early signal about potential performance bottlenecks, such as a slow downstream call, without waiting until the function is running in production to discover it through X-Ray traces there.

concepts.heading: Testing as a Deployment Gate, Not an Afterthought
concepts.body: Configuring CodePipeline so that a failed test stage genuinely blocks the pipeline (rather than just reporting a failure that a human might ignore) is what turns automated testing into an enforced deployment gate rather than a advisory step; this is why the pipeline's stage-to-stage failure propagation, discussed on Day 20, and the testing strategy discussed here are really two halves of the same safety mechanism.

examPoints: A scenario describing a developer who wants to test Lambda function logic quickly and repeatedly without deploying to AWS for each change is pointing to sam local invoke.

A scenario requiring that a failed integration test against a staging deployment automatically prevents a production deployment from happening is pointing to structuring CodePipeline with a dedicated test stage whose failure halts the pipeline, not to a manual process of checking test results separately.

quiz.q: A developer wants to test a Lambda function's business logic repeatedly during active development without deploying to AWS after every change. What should they use?
choices: Deploy to a staging environment for every code change
The SAM CLI's sam local invoke command
Manually test only after merging to the main branch
Test exclusively through the API Gateway console
quiz.explain: sam local invoke runs the function locally in a Lambda-like container for immediate feedback with no deployment required; deploying to staging for every change (choice A) would be far slower and defeats the purpose of fast local iteration.

quiz.q: A pipeline should automatically prevent a production deployment whenever integration tests against a freshly deployed staging environment fail. How should this be achieved?
choices: Skip testing and deploy directly to production
Add a dedicated automated test stage in CodePipeline after the staging deployment, so a failure halts the pipeline
Ask engineers to manually check staging before deploying to production
Only run unit tests during the build phase
quiz.explain: A dedicated test stage whose failure halts pipeline progression enforces this automatically and consistently; relying on engineers to manually check (choice C) is exactly the kind of human-dependent step CI/CD pipelines are meant to eliminate.

days.recap: sam local invoke enables fast, deployment-free Lambda testing, unit tests run during the build phase while integration tests need a real staging deployment, and a well-structured pipeline sequences both with stage failures blocking further progress.

days.title: Domain 3 Review: Deployment

concepts.heading: Packaging and IaC Recap
concepts.body: This domain begins with deployment artifacts (zip versus container images) and infrastructure-as-code tooling (SAM's serverless-focused simplicity and local testing versus CDK's general-purpose language and reusable Constructs), both of which ultimately rely on CloudFormation's stack, change set, and rollback mechanics underneath.

concepts.heading: CI/CD Pipeline Recap
concepts.body: CodePipeline orchestrates the source-build-test-deploy flow with optional manual approval gates, CodeBuild executes buildspec.yml-defined build phases in a fully managed environment, and CodeArtifact centralizes internal and proxied public package dependencies, together forming the automation backbone that turns a code commit into a running deployment without any team manually operating build servers or a package mirror.

concepts.heading: Deployment Strategy Recap
concepts.body: CodeDeploy's four deployment strategies, in-place, blue/green, canary, and linear, trade off infrastructure cost, deployment speed, and rollback safety differently, and CloudWatch alarm-triggered automatic rollback is what actually makes a gradual deployment self-protecting rather than merely slower, since a timer-based traffic shift alone still reaches 100% on a bad release without something actively watching for errors.

concepts.heading: Testing and the Full Deployment Sequence Recap
concepts.body: sam local invoke supports fast, deployment-free iteration during development, unit tests run cheaply during the CodeBuild build phase, and integration tests require a real staging deployment to exercise actual infrastructure, with a failure at any of these points halting the pipeline before a bad change can reach production.

examPoints: When a scenario specifies whether downtime is acceptable, whether automatic rollback on failure is required, and whether traffic needs to shift gradually or all at once, the correct CodeDeploy strategy usually becomes clear almost immediately.

When a scenario describes a pipeline stage catching a problem before the next stage runs, identify whether it's a unit test (build phase), an integration test (post-staging-deployment), or a manual approval (human judgment) to pick the right pipeline construct.

quiz.q: Which CloudFormation feature lets you preview exactly which resources will be added, modified, or replaced before actually applying a stack update?
choices: A nested stack
A change set
An Export value
A DeletionPolicy
quiz.explain: A change set computes and displays the impact of an update before it is executed, which is the standard safeguard against unexpected production changes.

quiz.q: Which Lambda deployment strategy shifts traffic to a new version in equal increments at equal time intervals until it reaches 100%?
choices: AllAtOnce
Canary
Linear
In-place
quiz.explain: Linear deployment increases traffic in fixed, repeated steps at regular intervals, whereas Canary makes one small initial shift followed by a single larger jump to 100%.

days.recap: Domain 3 wrap-up: SAM/CDK/CloudFormation form the IaC layer, CodePipeline/CodeBuild/CodeArtifact form the CI/CD layer, and CodeDeploy's four strategies plus alarm-based rollback determine how safely a new version reaches production.

days.title: Root Cause Analysis with Amazon CloudWatch

concepts.heading: Querying Logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights
concepts.body: CloudWatch Logs Insights provides a purpose-built query language for searching and aggregating across one or more log groups, letting you write a query like 'fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/ | stats count() by bin(5m)' to see exactly when and how often a specific error pattern occurred, without downloading or manually grepping through raw log files. Because Insights queries run against indexed log data on demand rather than requiring pre-configured metric filters, it is the fastest tool for ad hoc investigation once you already suspect something is wrong and need to confirm when it started and how widespread it is.

concepts.heading: CloudWatch Alarms: Static and Anomaly-Based
concepts.body: A CloudWatch alarm watches a single metric (or a math expression combining metrics) and transitions to ALARM state when a condition is met, which can then trigger an SNS notification, an Auto Scaling action, or a Lambda function automatically. Alarms can use a fixed static threshold (useful when you know the acceptable range in advance, like 'CPU above 80%') or Anomaly Detection, which builds a statistical model of a metric's expected range based on its historical pattern (including daily/weekly seasonality) and alarms when the actual value falls outside a configurable number of standard deviations from that band, which is better suited to metrics whose 'normal' value naturally varies by time of day.

concepts.heading: Custom Metrics and the Embedded Metric Format
concepts.body: Applications can publish their own business-level metrics, such as failed checkout attempts or orders per minute, directly to CloudWatch using the PutMetricData API, letting you build alarms and dashboards around metrics that matter to the business rather than only infrastructure-level metrics AWS provides by default. The Embedded Metric Format (EMF) offers a more efficient alternative: your application writes specially structured JSON log lines, and CloudWatch automatically extracts metrics from them without a separate PutMetricData API call per event, which reduces both API call volume and cost at high event throughput.

concepts.heading: Correlating Logs Across Distributed Services
concepts.body: In a distributed, multi-service architecture, a single end-user request may touch several Lambda functions, an API Gateway stage, and a database, each logging independently, so consistently generating and propagating a correlation ID (often the API Gateway request ID, or a custom trace ID) through every log statement related to that request lets you reconstruct the full path of a single request across services using a single Logs Insights query filtered on that ID. Without a shared correlation ID, diagnosing a single failed request across a distributed system reduces to manually cross-referencing timestamps, which is unreliable at any meaningful scale.

concepts.heading: CloudWatch Dashboards for At-a-Glance Health
concepts.body: CloudWatch Dashboards let you assemble metrics, alarms, and even Logs Insights query results from multiple services onto a single customizable view, which is commonly used to give an on-call engineer a single screen showing the health of an entire application (error rates, latency percentiles, queue depths) rather than needing to check each service's console individually during an incident.

examPoints: A scenario asking how to quickly determine when a specific error message started occurring and how frequently, across potentially large volumes of log data, is pointing to CloudWatch Logs Insights rather than manually searching individual log streams.

A scenario describing a need to monitor a business-level metric, like order failure rate, that AWS does not expose as a built-in metric, is pointing to publishing a custom metric via PutMetricData or using the Embedded Metric Format.

quiz.q: An on-call engineer needs to determine exactly when a specific error message began appearing in the last hour and how many times it occurred, across a large log group. What is the fastest approach?
choices: Manually download and search through raw log files
Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query filtering and aggregating on that error message
Use AWS X-Ray exclusively
Use Amazon CodeGuru Profiler
quiz.explain: Logs Insights is built specifically for fast, ad hoc filtering and aggregation across log groups; manually searching raw files (choice A) does not scale and would be far slower for this task.

quiz.q: A team wants to monitor a business metric, such as checkout failure rate, that has no equivalent built-in AWS metric. What should they do?
choices: Rely only on default EC2 CPU metrics
Publish a custom metric using PutMetricData or the Embedded Metric Format
Check AWS CloudTrail exclusively
Review VPC Flow Logs exclusively
quiz.explain: Custom metrics, published via PutMetricData or extracted automatically via EMF, let applications surface business-specific measurements directly in CloudWatch; CloudTrail (choice C) records API activity, not application-level business metrics.

days.recap: Logs Insights answers 'when and how often' questions about specific log patterns, alarms react to metrics using static or anomaly-based thresholds, custom metrics and EMF surface business-level data, and correlation IDs tie distributed logs back into one request's story.

days.title: Observability Instrumentation with AWS X-Ray

concepts.heading: Segments, Subsegments, and the X-Ray SDK
concepts.body: Instrumenting an application with the X-Ray SDK causes it to emit a segment for each service that processes part of a request (for example, one segment for a Lambda function's execution) and subsegments for individual operations within that segment, like an outbound call to DynamoDB or an external HTTP API, each recording start and end timestamps so the exact time spent in each step is measurable. Lambda functions can enable X-Ray tracing with a single configuration toggle to get basic automatic segments for the invocation and any instrumented AWS SDK calls, without hand-writing segment code for the built-in AWS SDK calls themselves.

concepts.heading: Traces as End-to-End Request Timelines
concepts.body: A trace stitches together every segment and subsegment generated by all the services a single request touched, identified by a shared trace ID that is propagated through HTTP headers (or messaging metadata) as the request moves between services, producing a single end-to-end timeline view that shows exactly where time was spent across the entire distributed call chain, not just within one function. This end-to-end view is what makes X-Ray fundamentally different from looking at each service's CloudWatch metrics or logs in isolation, since a single slow database call several hops deep would otherwise be invisible from the entry-point service's perspective alone.

concepts.heading: Annotations vs Metadata
concepts.body: Annotations are simple key-value pairs (strings, numbers, or booleans) attached to a segment that X-Ray indexes for searching and filtering, making them the right tool when you need to later find all traces matching a specific value, such as searching for every trace belonging to a particular customer ID or order ID. Metadata, in contrast, can hold arbitrarily complex, nested data (like a full request payload) for context when viewing a specific trace, but it is not indexed and therefore cannot be used as a search filter, so metadata is for detail-on-inspection while annotations are for query-and-find.

concepts.heading: The X-Ray Service Map
concepts.body: X-Ray automatically builds a visual Service Map showing every service that has processed traced requests as a node, with edges representing calls between them, and it visually highlights nodes with elevated error rates or unusually high average latency, which lets an engineer glance at the map during an incident and immediately identify which specific service in a complex chain is the likely bottleneck or failure point, rather than having to check every service's dashboard individually.

concepts.heading: Sampling Rules and Cost Control
concepts.body: Tracing every single request in a high-throughput system would generate significant data volume and cost, so X-Ray applies configurable sampling rules that trace only a percentage of requests (with a reservoir of always-traced requests per second to guarantee visibility even at low absolute traffic), and these rules can be customized to always trace higher-value paths, such as failed requests or specific critical endpoints, while sampling more sparingly on high-volume, low-risk traffic.

examPoints: A scenario requiring the ability to later search for all traces related to a specific customer or order ID is pointing to adding that value as an X-Ray annotation, since only annotations (not metadata) are indexed for search.

A scenario describing a distributed system spanning multiple microservices where the team needs to visually identify which specific service is the source of elevated latency or errors is pointing to the X-Ray Service Map.

quiz.q: A support team frequently needs to pull up every X-Ray trace associated with a specific customer ID to investigate reported issues. How should the customer ID be recorded on the trace?
choices: As X-Ray metadata only
As an X-Ray annotation
In application logs only, with no X-Ray involvement
As a subsegment name
quiz.explain: Annotations are indexed by X-Ray and can be used to filter and search traces, which is exactly what's needed here; metadata (choice A) is not indexed and cannot be searched on.

quiz.q: A system composed of many microservices is experiencing intermittent slow responses, and the team wants to visually pinpoint which specific service is causing the delay. What X-Ray feature should they use?
choices: CloudWatch basic dashboards only
The X-Ray Service Map
Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer
AWS Certificate Manager
quiz.explain: The Service Map visually highlights nodes with elevated latency or error rates across the entire distributed call chain, making the bottleneck visually apparent; CodeGuru Reviewer (choice C, closed to new customers since 2025-11-07) analyzes source code for issues, not live distributed request latency.

days.recap: The X-Ray SDK generates segments and subsegments that combine into end-to-end traces, annotations are indexed for search while metadata is for detailed inspection only, and the Service Map visually surfaces which service in a chain is the bottleneck.

days.title: Code Quality and Runtime Optimization with Amazon CodeGuru

concepts.heading: Automated Code Review with Amazon Q Developer
concepts.body: Amazon Q Developer code reviews use generative AI to automatically analyze code, surfacing findings such as potential resource leaks, concurrency bugs, hardcoded credentials and other secrets, input validation gaps, and deviations from AWS best practices, either on demand in the IDE or automatically when a pull request is opened through its GitHub integration, where findings are posted as comments directly on the pull request. Running on every pull request without requiring a human reviewer to remember to invoke it adds a consistent layer of automated review before a human reviewer even looks at the change, and Amazon Inspector can additionally scan connected code repositories for security vulnerabilities. Its predecessor, Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer, has been closed to new customers since 2025-11-07 (no new repository associations), so it is no longer the service to pick for a new setup.

concepts.heading: CodeGuru Profiler for Runtime Performance
concepts.body: Amazon CodeGuru Profiler continuously profiles a running production application's CPU usage and captures which functions and call paths ('hot paths') are consuming the most CPU time, using a lightweight agent that adds minimal overhead so it can safely run continuously in production rather than only during isolated benchmark runs. Because it profiles actual production traffic and workload patterns rather than a synthetic test, it often surfaces optimization opportunities that would never appear under artificial load testing conditions.

concepts.heading: Reading a Flame Graph
concepts.body: Profiler visualizes its findings as a flame graph, where each horizontal bar represents a function call, its width represents the proportion of total CPU time it consumed, and stacked bars above it represent the functions it called in turn, so the widest bars (regardless of vertical position) point directly to the functions consuming the most cumulative CPU time and are the best candidates for optimization effort. Learning to read a flame graph quickly, scanning for the widest bars rather than reading every label top to bottom, is a practical skill for interpreting Profiler's output efficiently.

concepts.heading: Cost and Performance Benefits of Profiling
concepts.body: Because compute cost in Lambda and EC2 both scale with CPU/execution time, identifying and optimizing a genuinely hot code path found by Profiler frequently produces both a latency improvement for end users and a direct reduction in compute cost, making Profiler a tool that pays for itself through cost savings alone in high-traffic applications even before considering the user experience benefit.

concepts.heading: How CodeGuru Fits Into the Broader Development Lifecycle
concepts.body: Amazon Q Developer code reviews operate before code is even merged (at the pull-request stage), catching correctness and security issues early and cheaply, while CodeGuru Profiler operates continuously in the running production system, catching performance issues that only manifest under real traffic; together they cover both the 'is this code correct and secure' and the 'is this code fast enough in practice' questions at two different points in the software lifecycle.

examPoints: A scenario describing a desire for automatic, machine-learning-driven code review comments on every pull request, catching bugs and security issues before a human reviewer looks at the change, is pointing to Amazon Q Developer code reviews (Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer is closed to new customers since 2025-11-07).
A scenario asking how to identify which specific function is consuming the most CPU time in a live production application is pointing to Amazon CodeGuru Profiler and its flame graph visualization.

quiz.q: A team wants every pull request automatically scanned by machine learning for potential bugs, resource leaks, and security issues, with findings posted as comments on the PR itself. Which service should they use?
choices: Amazon CodeGuru Profiler
Amazon Q Developer code reviews
AWS X-Ray
CloudWatch Logs Insights
quiz.explain: Amazon Q Developer code reviews run automatically when a pull request is opened and post AI-driven findings as comments on it (its predecessor, CodeGuru Reviewer, is closed to new customers since 2025-11-07); CodeGuru Profiler (choice A) analyzes runtime performance in production, not pull request code.

quiz.q: A production application's compute costs are higher than expected, and the team wants to identify exactly which function is consuming the most CPU time under real traffic. What should they use?
choices: CodeGuru Reviewer
CodeGuru Profiler and its flame graph
AWS WAF
Amazon ECR image scanning
quiz.explain: CodeGuru Profiler continuously profiles live production CPU usage and visualizes hot paths in a flame graph, directly identifying optimization targets; CodeGuru Reviewer (choice A, closed to new customers since 2025-11-07) analyzes static source code, not live runtime CPU consumption.

days.recap: Amazon Q Developer code reviews catch bugs, leaks, and security issues at pull-request time using AI (replacing CodeGuru Reviewer, now closed to new customers), CodeGuru Profiler continuously identifies CPU-hungry hot paths in production visualized as flame graphs, and together they cover correctness and performance at two distinct stages of the lifecycle.

days.title: Domain 4 Review and Full Four-Week Synthesis

concepts.heading: The Diagnostic Layering of Domain 4
concepts.body: This domain's three tools form a natural diagnostic hierarchy for troubleshooting: CloudWatch Logs Insights and alarms tell you what is happening and when, X-Ray traces and the Service Map tell you where in a distributed call chain the problem is occurring, and CodeGuru Profiler tells you why a specific piece of code is slow at the CPU-cycle level, so a mature troubleshooting workflow moves through these three tools in that order rather than jumping straight to source code.

concepts.heading: Automated Code Review as a Complementary, Earlier Check
concepts.body: Unlike the other three tools in this domain which all operate on a running system, automated code review (Amazon Q Developer code reviews; the older CodeGuru Reviewer is closed to new customers since 2025-11-07) operates before deployment at the pull-request stage, which is worth remembering distinctly since exam scenarios about 'catching an issue before it reaches production' point to automated code review, while scenarios about 'diagnosing an issue already happening in production' point to CloudWatch, X-Ray, or Profiler depending on the specific symptom described.

concepts.heading: Tying the Four Domains Together
concepts.body: Across the full 28 days, Domain 1 covers building the application itself (compute, data stores, messaging), Domain 2 covers securing it (authentication, encryption, secrets), Domain 3 covers getting it into production reliably (infrastructure as code, CI/CD, deployment strategies), and Domain 4 covers keeping it healthy once it's live (observability and optimization), and recognizing which of these four concerns a scenario is actually describing is often the single fastest way to narrow four answer choices down to two before even reading them closely.

concepts.heading: A Final Word on Confusable Pairs Across All Four Domains
concepts.body: Nearly every domain contains at least one pair of services that sound similar but solve different problems: GSI versus LSI, SNS versus SQS, Secrets Manager versus Parameter Store, canary versus linear deployment, and CloudWatch versus X-Ray versus CodeGuru Profiler are the highest-yield pairs to have completely solid before exam day, since a large share of scenario questions are really just testing whether you can tell two similar-sounding services apart under time pressure.

examPoints: When a scenario describes a symptom (slow, erroring, or expensive) rather than naming a tool directly, work through the diagnostic order of CloudWatch (what/when) to X-Ray (where) to CodeGuru Profiler (why) to identify which tool the question is actually testing.

Across all four domains, a recurring correct-answer pattern is choosing the AWS-managed, serverless-native option that removes undifferentiated operational work from the developer, rather than a manually-managed alternative.

quiz.q: Which AWS service visually traces a request's path and latency across multiple microservices in a distributed system?
choices: CloudWatch Logs Insights
AWS X-Ray
Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer
AWS WAF
quiz.explain: X-Ray is purpose-built for distributed tracing and visualizes the full request path via its Service Map, spanning multiple services in a single view; CodeGuru Reviewer (closed to new customers since 2025-11-07) reviews source code, not live requests.

quiz.q: Across the four exam domains, which one carries the largest single share of exam weight?
choices: Domain 1: Development with AWS Services (32%)
Domain 2: Security (26%)
Domain 3: Deployment (24%)
Domain 4: Troubleshooting and Optimization (18%)
quiz.explain: Development with AWS Services carries the largest weighting at 32%, making it the highest-leverage domain for focused review time.

days.recap: Domain 4 wrap-up: CloudWatch answers what/when, X-Ray answers where, and CodeGuru Profiler answers why at the code level, while automated code review (Amazon Q Developer) catches issues earlier at the pull-request stage; overall, the four domains map to building, securing, shipping, and operating the application.

days.title: Final Day: Full-Length Practice Exam and Test-Day Checklist

concepts.heading: Simulating Real Exam Conditions
concepts.body: Take one full-length, cross-domain practice exam (65 questions, 130 minutes) under realistic timed conditions, using either AWS Skill Builder's official practice exam or a reputable third-party question bank, sitting through the entire exam in one sitting without pausing, exactly as the real test will be administered, so that pacing and endurance are also being tested and not just knowledge.

concepts.heading: Reviewing Commonly Confused Service Pairs
concepts.body: Build a targeted error log from every missed question, and specifically re-drill the service pairs candidates most often confuse under exam pressure: GSI versus LSI, SNS versus SQS versus EventBridge, Secrets Manager versus Parameter Store, Canary versus Linear deployment, and Cognito authorizer versus Lambda authorizer, since these pairwise distinctions account for a disproportionate share of missed questions relative to how conceptually simple each pair actually is once clearly understood.

concepts.heading: DVA-C02's Emphasis on Practical, Code-Level Detail
concepts.body: This exam leans more heavily on concrete implementation detail than some other associate-level AWS exams, frequently embedding short code snippets, IAM policy fragments, or CLI/SDK configuration excerpts directly into questions, so effective final review means being able to recognize specific API calls (like TransactWriteItems or AssumeRole) and configuration keys (like maxAttempts or ReservedConcurrentExecutions) by sight, not just recalling a service's name and general purpose.

concepts.heading: A Weighted Final Review Pass
concepts.body: With limited remaining study time, allocate it proportionally to the exam's own domain weighting: spend the most remaining time on Domain 1 (32%, development with AWS services), then Domain 2 (26%, security), then Domain 3 (24%, deployment), and the least on Domain 4 (18%, troubleshooting and optimization), reviewing weak areas identified from the practice exam's missed questions within each domain rather than re-reading everything uniformly.

examPoints: In the final study session, time is better spent locking in the distinction between genuinely confusable service pairs than trying to learn any new service from scratch this late in preparation.

Use the exam's 'flag for review' feature liberally on any question involving an unfamiliar code, CLI, or configuration snippet, answer with your best guess to avoid leaving it blank, and return to flagged questions only after completing a full first pass through the exam.

quiz.q: During the DVA-C02 exam, a question includes a short code or configuration snippet as part of the scenario. What is the most effective approach?
choices: Skip reading the snippet and guess based on the question text alone
Carefully identify which specific API call or configuration setting the snippet uses, then match that to the answer choices
Always choose the shortest answer choice
Assume all code snippets are irrelevant distractions
quiz.explain: DVA-C02 frequently tests whether you can recognize a specific API or setting from a snippet, so carefully parsing it is essential to eliminating wrong answers; skipping it (choice A) discards the most important information the question provides.

quiz.q: With limited time remaining before the exam, what is the most effective use of final review time?
choices: Learning an entirely new AWS service not yet studied
Reviewing commonly confused service pairs and allocating remaining time proportionally to each domain's exam weight
Staying up all night reviewing every note from scratch
Skipping review entirely and relying on intuition
quiz.explain: Targeted review of confusable pairs and weighting remaining time by domain percentage maximizes score improvement per minute spent; learning an entirely new service this late (choice A) is a lower-value use of scarce remaining time.

days.recap: Final day: one full timed practice exam, a targeted review of commonly confused service pairs, close attention to code and configuration snippets, and a weighted final pass through the domains by their exam percentage.
